[Development blog](https://bwalletx.com/blog) · 021 · 7 Oct 2026 · Chat on BSV, part 1

# Coordinate on BSV

Big platforms put every community in one room. BSV needs a place to plan that it controls. Chat in bWalletX is that place: the first post in a series on chat on BSV.

## Why coordination matters

A currency is a shared agreement. It is worth something because enough people accept it, build on it and plan around it. That takes talking. Developers need to agree on standards. Merchants need to know who else takes it. Token holders need to find each other. New people need somewhere to ask questions and get a straight answer.

A community that can’t talk can’t act together. It can still have good technology. But nobody ships the second app that uses the first one, nobody lists the token, and nobody shows up when it matters. Coordination is not a nice extra. It is how the work gets joined up.

## How the conversation got scattered

For most crypto communities, the conversation happens on Twitter, Reddit and Telegram. That is where people are. It works because everyone is in one room.

It is also the problem. When every community shares one room, a small community with a contested history sits next to a much larger one that wants it gone. BSV split from Bitcoin Cash in November 2018, which itself split from Bitcoin in 2017. Each split left people angry at each other, and the arguments never really stopped.

In April 2019 a #DelistBSV campaign spread on Twitter. It followed legal threats from BSV’s best-known backer against a pseudonymous critic, and the anger was not all unearned. But it was aimed at the coin and everyone building on it. Binance, Kraken and ShapeShift delisted BSV that month ([Bitcoin Magazine](https://bitcoinmagazine.com/markets/binance-delists-bitcoin-sv), [Finance Magnates](https://www.financemagnates.com/cryptocurrency/news/kraken-follows-binance-to-delist-bitcoin-sv/), [The Next Web](https://thenextweb.com/news/binance-delist-bitcoinsv-cryptocurrency)). Kraken ran a Twitter poll before deciding. Since then, BSV threads on the big platforms have often drawn pile-ons and ridicule from some prominent BTC advocates and from organised campaigns. Not from everyone who holds BTC. Most people don’t care either way. But a small, loud group is enough to make a room useless for planning.

The effect is easy to see. Many BSV builders and users stopped posting in public. The ones who stayed are spread across a dozen group chats and a handful of accounts. A newcomer who searches for BSV finds the argument, not the work.

Do the platforms themselves push BSV down? Maybe. We can’t show it, so we won’t claim it. It doesn’t change the answer. Even a perfectly neutral feed ranks what gets the most reactions, and a pile-on gets a lot of reactions.

## BSV is a messaging protocol

Every Bitcoin transaction can carry data. On BSV that data can be large and cheap, so a transaction can be a message: a post, a reply, a like, a payment with a note on it. Sending money and sending a message are the same act.

People have built on that for years. Memo and Twetch put social posts on chain. Treechat built threaded discussion. Peck reads posts written in Bitcoin Schema. Fwetch posts to boards on the Vulpine network. These apps came and went at different times, and some are still running. They prove the point: BSV was a social network before anyone called it one.

What was missing was one place that holds your money, your identity and your conversations together, and that reads the other apps instead of competing with them.

## Why paid, signed messages change things

On an ad-funded platform, attention is free to take. An account costs nothing, a reply costs nothing, and a hundred replies cost nothing. The platform makes money from the reactions either way. That is why a pile-on is cheap to start and hard to stop.

Change two things and the sums change. First, tie every account to a wallet, so a name has a history and a balance behind it. Second, let the receiver set a price. A friend messages you free. A stranger pays a few cents. A thousand strangers pay a thousand times that, and the money goes to the person they are shouting at. Nobody needs to moderate a pile-on that pays its target.

This is not new thinking. Hashcash, the proof-of-work idea Bitcoin borrowed, was first proposed in 1997 as a way to make email spam cost something. Small payments on BSV let us do the same thing with real money instead of burnt computation.

## Advertise there, coordinate here

We are not leaving Twitter, Reddit or Telegram. New people are there, and we want them. So we keep posting there: news, releases, links.

But the planning happens somewhere else. On BSV-native rooms, where every account is a wallet. That changes the cost of bad behaviour. A throwaway account costs nothing on Twitter. In a token room you have to hold the token to get in. And once rooms can charge per message, and you can set a price for strangers to reach you, spam and pile-ons cost money. Brigading a room gets expensive. Talking with friends stays free.

That is the rule: advertise there, coordinate here.

## Where we are taking this

A rule like that is only useful if there is a “here”. So we built Chat into bWalletX, with bChat as the full version on the web. Your wallet is your account. Rooms, private messages and calls sit next to your coins and tokens. Some of it is live, and the paid parts are still being built. What works today, and what doesn’t yet, is on [bwalletx.com/chat](https://bwalletx.com/chat).

The tools matter less than the habit. If BSV people plan in BSV rooms, and point to them from everywhere else, the conversation stops depending on a feed that someone else ranks. Start a room for your project. Post the link on Twitter. Then go back to the room and do the work. App builders can let users sign in with their wallet: [bwalletx.com/connect](https://bwalletx.com/connect).

— Richard

## Next in this series

- Token rooms: hold to enter

- Paying to be heard: priced messages and calls

- Pay-per-second calls and streams

- Private messages and keys

- Message boards versus feeds

- Agents in chat

Related: [Chat in bWalletX](https://bwalletx.com/chat) · [005 Personal tokens and token rooms](https://bwalletx.com/blog/005-personal-tokens-and-rooms) · [014 One feed for BSV](https://bwalletx.com/blog/014-open-feed) · [017 Sign in with bWalletX, and the Lounge](https://bwalletx.com/blog/017-sign-in-and-lounge)

[← 020 Sign in with X](https://bwalletx.com/blog/020-sign-in-with-x)[022 Bring your coins home →](https://bwalletx.com/blog/022-bring-your-coins-home)

---

Source: https://bwalletx.com/blog/022-bring-your-coins-home

[Development blog](https://bwalletx.com/blog) · 022 · 7 Oct 2026

# Bring your coins home

BSV coins sit in wallets that closed, changed hands or changed their paths. The 12 words still work. How bWalletX restores or sweeps them, and what has to stay behind.

## Why coins end up scattered

Most people who have used BSV for a few years have used more than one wallet. Each app came with its own wallet, and each wallet made its own set of keys. You tried one for tipping, another for a game, another for a social site. A few cents here, a few dollars there.

Then the wallets changed. Some shut down. Money Button closed in 2022, and its website went with it. Others changed hands and were rebuilt. Some changed how they turn your words into keys, so a newer version of the same wallet looks in a different place from the older one. The coins never moved. The app that knew where to look for them did.

So the money is still there, on chain, on addresses nobody opens any more. What’s missing is a wallet that knows where to look.

## Why the 12 words still work

A recovery phrase is not a password stored on someone’s server. It is a large random number written as words. Every key the wallet ever used is worked out from that number by a fixed recipe, and the recipe is public. The steps are called a derivation path, and they look like `m/44'/236'/0'/0/0`.

That means the words don’t depend on the company that gave them to you. If you know the words and the path the wallet used, any wallet can work out the same keys, today or in ten years. The only hard part is the path. Every wallet picked its own, and few of them wrote it down where users would see it.

bWalletX knows the paths used by the wallets in its family tree and by the common standards, and it tries all of them for you.

## Restoring and sweeping are different

Restoring opens the old wallet as an account in bWalletX. It is the same keys, so nothing moves on chain and nothing is paid. Your coins, ordinals and tokens show up because bWalletX is now looking at the same addresses. This works when the old wallet used a small, known set of keys, as Yours, Panda, RelayX and Twetch do.

Sweeping moves what’s in the old wallet into an account you already have. bWalletX walks through the old wallet’s addresses, finds everything on them, and sends it to you in new transactions. That costs a small network fee. It is the right choice for wallets that spread coins over many addresses, like SimplyCash, or when you want everything in one account and the old words retired.

You don’t need to know which wallet the words came from. The sweep screen takes a phrase, a private key or an xprv in one box and tries every layout it knows.

## Which wallets

The full list, with the paths and what each needs, is on [bwalletx.com/restore](https://bwalletx.com/restore). In short: bWalletX, Yours and Panda, RelayX and Twetch can be restored as accounts. SimplyCash and other 12 or 24-word wallets can be swept. Private keys and xprvs work too, and you can type a custom path for anything else. Money Button can be swept too, since 5.1.83.

## What can’t come across

Not everything on an old wallet can be moved by the person who holds the words. The clearest case is Money Button’s tokens.

Money Button tokens used a protocol called SFP. Each token sits in a small output that can only be spent with two signatures: yours and the token server’s. The server checked every transfer and signed it. When Money Button closed, the server went too. Your key is still valid, but the second signature can never come. Nobody can move these tokens, and nobody can burn them either.

The danger is a sweep that doesn’t know this. A token output carries a few hundred satoshis, so a careless sweep sees it as spare BSV and tries to spend it. At best that fails. bWalletX recognises SFP outputs, keeps them out of the BSV sweep, and lists them so you know they’re there. They stay safe where they are, in case there is ever a way to honour them.

A few other things are not swept today: names, BSV-20 tokens and locked coins. The sweep screen counts them and tells you. If you restore the wallet as an account instead, they stay visible in bWalletX.

## A true story

While building the Money Button import, we tested it on an old phrase from 2020, written down and then forgotten. The wallet that made it no longer exists. bWalletX walked Money Button’s path and found 31 used addresses. On them were a little BSV and 13 old Money Button tokens.

The BSV came across in one sweep. The 13 tokens were found, named and left alone, which is the only safe thing to do with them. A phrase that had been dead for years was a working wallet again in a couple of minutes.

## Stay safe

- Never type your words into a website. Not a “wallet recovery” site, not a form, not a chat, not a support agent. Anyone who has your words has your coins. Type them only into the wallet app itself.

- Everything is worked out on your device. bWalletX derives every key on your phone or computer. The words are never sent anywhere, and after a sweep they are not kept.

- A sweep is final. It sends coins in new transactions to your account. Check what the scan found before you confirm.

- Start small. bWalletX is in beta. If an old wallet holds a lot, sweep a small one first and see how it goes.

If your old wallet isn’t found, [tell us which one](mailto:support@bwalletx.com?subject=Restore%20from%20another%20wallet). We’ll add the path if we can find it.

Related: [Restore into bWalletX](https://bwalletx.com/restore) · [001 Forking Yours Wallet onto phones](https://bwalletx.com/blog/001-the-fork)

[Development blog](https://bwalletx.com/blog) · 023 · 7 Oct 2026

# Locks you can’t break

Lock BSV until a date, or as payouts over time, and nobody can unlock it early, not even you. Why that is useful, how BSV enforces it with no custodian, and where the limits are.

Status: live since 5.1.84. Lock BSV is in the app now. It is a new feature, so start small: lock only small amounts until it has been out for a while. The app asks again above 0.01 BSV.

## Why you would want to lose access to your own money

Most of what a wallet does is make money easier to move. A lock does the opposite on purpose. You decide now, while you are calm, what you are allowed to do later. Then the decision can’t be undone.

That sounds like a restriction, and it is. It is useful for the same reason a fixed-term deposit or a savings jar with no slot to get coins out is useful:

- Commitment. If you can’t touch it, you can’t spend it on a bad day.

- Savings discipline. Put an amount away for a year and stop thinking about it.

- Paying yourself a salary. Lock a sum and have it come back as $10 a day, or 0.1 BSV a week, instead of all at once.

- Vesting. A founder or a team can lock their own coins on a schedule, the way shares vest.

- Proving you can’t dump. If people worry that you will sell, you can show them coins that you can’t move until a date they can check for themselves.

## How BSV enforces it, with nobody holding the keys

Usually, “nobody can touch it until next year” means a bank or an exchange holds the money and promises not to give it back early. You trust them to keep that promise, and to still exist.

A BSV lock doesn’t need anyone in the middle. The coins stay on your own key, in an output with a small script attached. It is the same lock script Hodlocker made popular and that Yours Wallet and the 1Sat tools already use; we didn’t write a new one. To spend that output, a transaction has to show the script its own contents, and the script checks two things in it: that it is signed by your key, and that its lock time is at least a block height written into the script. The network will not accept a transaction with a lock time in the future. So the coins can’t move until that block exists, and after that only your key can move them.

Every miner checks this, every time. bWalletX has no override. We tested it by running the script through an interpreter: spending one block early fails, spending with someone else’s key fails, and spending at the height with your key works.

## How a schedule works

You can lock everything until one date, or set up gradual payouts. For payouts, the wallet splits the amount into pieces and locks each one to a later height, all in one transaction. You choose daily, weekly, monthly or every few days, and either a number of payouts or an end date.

Each payout can be sized three ways:

- Dollars, the default: “$10 a day”. You still lock BSV. Each piece is sized at today’s price plus a buffer, 20% unless you change it, so that it usually still covers $10 later. When a piece opens, your wallet looks up that day’s price and pays out $10 worth. Any extra can go back into the next piece as a fresh lock, if you approve it. If the price has fallen past the buffer, you get the whole piece and the schedule says so: “paid $8.40 of $10”. If the wallet can’t get a price, it doesn’t guess. The piece stays in your wallet as BSV.

- BSV: 0.1 BSV a week, say.

- A percentage: of the original amount, which pays the same each time and ends after 100÷X payouts (0.01% a day takes about 27 years), or of what is left, which pays less each time and finishes the small remainder in one go.

Before you lock, you see every payout in a table: the estimated date, the block height, the BSV and roughly what it is worth today. Then you type LOCK.

When pieces open, the Locks screen shows them as ready. One tap claims every opened piece, across all your locks, in one transaction.

## A receipt anyone can check

For the “prove you can’t dump” case, you can mint a public receipt. It is an NFT, made in the same transaction as the locks, showing the amount, the schedule and who locked it. It ends with “Verify at bwalletx.com/lock/verify”.

The picture on its own proves nothing. Anyone can make an image that says “100 BSV locked”. What matters is the check. The [verify page](https://bwalletx.com/lock/verify) reads the transaction from the chain, decodes every lock output, and confirms that each payout the receipt claims is a real lock with that height and that amount, all to one key. It also checks whether each piece has been claimed yet: Locked, Partly claimed or Fully claimed. A receipt that claims more than the transaction holds, or a later date than the script enforces, is flagged.

The receipt is off by default. It ties your name to an amount, in public, for good, so only turn it on if that is what you want.

## The limits

- It is irreversible. That is the point, but it means a typo is permanent. The wallet won’t lock any piece for more than about ten years, and makes you confirm.

- It is BSV, not dollars. The dollar figures are targets worked out in your own wallet. They are not guarantees, and nothing here is a promise about the price.

- Dates are approximate. A lock opens at a block height, about 144 blocks a day. Blocks don’t arrive exactly every ten minutes.

- Your 12 words are the only way back. If you lose them, nobody can recover the locks. Not us, not anyone.

- Small pieces aren’t worth it. Claiming a piece costs a small fee, so each payout must be at least 1,000 sats. If a percentage gives smaller pieces, the wallet suggests paying out less often.

- Very long schedules come in batches. One transaction holds up to 520 payouts. Beyond that, the later payouts are kept in one lock that the wallet offers to re-split when it opens.

Everything about it is on [bwalletx.com/lock](https://bwalletx.com/lock).

Related: [Lock BSV](https://bwalletx.com/lock) · [Verify a lock](https://bwalletx.com/lock/verify) · [016 Subscriptions, paid from pots](https://bwalletx.com/blog/016-pots)

Source: https://bwalletx.com/blog/024-tips-and-paid-likes

[Development blog](https://bwalletx.com/blog) · 024 · 7 Oct 2026

# Pay the person who wrote it

Tips and paid likes in bWalletX 5.1.72: the payment goes to the author in the same transaction as the like. Why bChat takes 0%, why the home app gets 5% on top, and how authors can hide their own posts.

Status: out in bWalletX 5.1.72.

## A like costs nothing, so it is worth nothing

On most social apps a like is free. You tap a heart, a number goes up, and the person who wrote the post gets nothing they can use. The platform gets something: a signal it can sell to advertisers. Writers who want to be paid have to go somewhere else, to a tip jar, a subscription site or a payment app, and ask readers to follow them there. Most readers don’t.

The gap between “I liked this” and “I paid for this” is a few extra steps, and that is where most of the money gets lost. Every extra screen, every separate account and every card form loses people who would have paid a few cents if it were as easy as tapping a heart.

In the bChat feed inside bWalletX, a like can carry money, and a tip is one tap. The payment goes to the person who wrote the post, in the same transaction as the like. There is no second step and no separate account.

## What happens when you tap

There are two actions.

- Paid like. A like with a payment attached. The default is 1,000 sats, and you can change it. It still counts as a like, once per person.

- Tip. You pick an amount. The presets are in dollars, $0.05, $0.25 and $1, converted to sats at the current rate. The smallest tip is 546 sats, and one tip can’t be more than 1 BSV, so a typo can’t empty your wallet.

Either way, your wallet builds one Bitcoin transaction with two parts next to each other. The first is the record: “this is a like (or a tip) for post X, of amount A”, signed by you. The second is the payment: exactly A sats to the author’s address. Your change comes back to you, and the network fee is the normal small one.

Because both parts are in one transaction, they can’t come apart. There is no like that says it was paid when the payment failed, and no payment that lost track of what it was for. Anyone reading the chain can check that the payment output pays the author exactly the amount the record says. The feed only counts a tip towards a post’s total when that check passes. Anything else counts as zero.

## The author gets the money, not the app

The payment goes to the address that signed the post. For a bChat post, that is the author’s own signing address. For a Twetch post, it is the address of the author’s Twetch key, the one that signs their posts. The money arrives in their wallet whatever app they use, because it is just a Bitcoin payment and needs nobody’s cooperation.

There is one exception, and we refuse it outright. Treechat signs every post with one shared key, so the signing address belongs to Treechat, not to the person who wrote the post. A tip there would go to Treechat. So for Treechat posts the wallet shows that tips are unavailable, and the builder throws an error rather than paying. When Treechat publishes a payment address for each author, that can change.

Unliking doesn’t refund. If you paid-like a post and then unlike it, the like goes away and the payment stays with the author. That is how a payment works: once it is sent, it is theirs.

## Why bChat takes 0%

The format allows the app you are using to add a fee of its own: up to 5% of the amount and never more than 10,000 sats, as a separate output, never taken from the author’s share. bChat sets its fee to zero. With a zero fee, no fee output is written at all.

We did that on purpose. bChat shows posts from other BSV apps as well as its own. If we took a cut of every tip on someone else’s post, we would be doing what we complain about in big platforms: standing between the writer and the reader and charging for it. The point of the feed is that it is open. It is easier to ask other apps to join an open feed when we aren’t charging tolls on it. bWalletX makes its money in other places.

## Why the home app gets 5%, on top

When you tip or paid-like a post that was written in another app, Twetch or Peck for example, bChat adds 5% of the amount on top for that app. If you tip 10,000 sats, the author still gets exactly 10,000 sats, and the home app gets 500 more as its own output. It is capped at 10,000 sats. The wallet’s approval screen lists it as its own line, so you see what you are paying before you sign.

The reason is simple. That app found the writer, hosted the conversation and built the thing people came to read. bChat is showing its post to new readers. Sending a share back is the fair thing to do, and it gives other apps a reason to want their posts shown in an open feed instead of a reason to fight it.

There are rules. The share only goes to an address the home app has published for itself. We never guess one, and we never use a shared relay key. It is never paid to the author’s address or the fee address, and never on bChat’s own posts. Today no app has published one yet, so in practice the share is not being paid. When an app publishes its address, the share switches on for its posts, with no new release needed.

## Authors stay in control: hiding your own post

Paying people for posts makes posts matter more, and that makes it more important that authors can change their minds. Posts on BSV are on chain and can’t be deleted. What an author can do in bWalletX is ask for a post to be hidden.

“Hide my post” writes a small signed record: “hide post X”. The feed honours it only when it is signed by the same key that signed the post, so nobody else can hide your posts, and you can’t hide anyone else’s. The latest of hide and unhide wins, so you can undo it. The indexer checks each signature, and the feed leaves hidden posts out.

Hiding happens when the feed is read. The post is still on chain, and another app can still show it. We can’t promise more than that, and we don’t pretend to. It is the same model every app in the open feed uses: each one runs its own filters and moderation on top of the shared data. For the same reason as tips, this doesn’t work for Treechat posts, because there is no per-author key to check.

## What it changes

When liking and paying are the same action, the signal means something. A post with a hundred paid likes was worth real money to a hundred people. That is harder to fake than a hundred free taps, and it goes straight to the writer, not to the platform. A writer doesn’t need a sponsorship deal or a paywall to get something back for a good post. They need readers who can pay as easily as they can like.

It is small money per tap. That is the point. Bitcoin SV fees are low enough that a few cents can move on its own, and a wallet built into the feed means nobody has to leave to pay.

More about the feed, tips and your handle on the [Social page](https://bwalletx.com/social).

Related: [014 One feed for BSV](https://bwalletx.com/blog/014-open-feed) · [019 Blur slurs, show swearing](https://bwalletx.com/blog/019-language-filter) · [Chat](https://bwalletx.com/chat)

# Push notifications, from our own server

Since bWalletX 5.1.70, phones, the web wallet and the extension get push notifications from push.bwalletx.com. What notifies you, what the server knows and doesn’t, and what it costs.

Status: out in bWalletX 5.1.70, on iPhone and Android, in the web wallet and in the Chrome extension.

## A wallet with chat needs to tap you on the shoulder

bWalletX has chat built in: token rooms, DMs, calls and b, the assistant. Chat that only works while the app is open isn’t much use. If a friend sends you a message, you should find out without having to check. That needs push notifications.

The usual way to add them is to sign up for a notification company, drop its SDK into the app and send it everything: who your users are, who is messaging whom, and often the text of the messages. It is quick to set up, and it means a third party ends up with a list of your users’ conversations.

We didn’t want that, so we run our own small push server at `push.bwalletx.com`.

## What notifies you

- Direct messages. Always, unless you turn that conversation off.

- Mentions. When someone mentions you in a room, unless you turn that room off.

- Group messages. Only if you ask for them. Each room has a bell with three settings: All, Mentions and Off. Groups start on Mentions, so a busy room doesn’t buzz your phone all day.

- Calls. An incoming call rings through.

- Answers from b. When the assistant replies in a room.

Tapping a notification opens the room or DM it is about.

Two more rules keep it calm. If a room gets busy, you get one notification per room every 30 seconds at most, and the next one says “N new messages in X” instead of one buzz per line. And you can set quiet hours, which hold back everything except calls.

Your preview setting and quiet hours belong to your account, not to one device, so they follow you from your phone to the web wallet to the extension. The settings are in Settings › Notifications › Push notifications.

## What the server knows

To send you a notification, the server has to know a few things, and it keeps only those:

- Your handle and your devices. For each device: the platform (iPhone, Android, web or extension) and the push token Apple, Google or your browser gave it. That token is an address for a device, nothing more.

- Your settings. Previews on or off, quiet hours and your time zone, and the bell setting for each room you have changed.

You register by signing in with your wallet, the same signed proof bChat uses. There is no email address and no password. If you turn notifications off, or sign out, the device is removed.

## What it doesn’t know

The push server doesn’t read your rooms. When a message is sent, bChat, which already knows who is in each room, tells the server who should be told and passes a short preview. The server decides who gets a notification, sends it and forgets it. No message text is ever stored. Its database has a devices table and a settings table, and that is all. Its log line for each event says the kind of event and how many devices it went to. It doesn’t log who sent what to whom.

Previews are off by default. With previews off, the text of the message never leaves our server. The notification says “$alice sent you a message” or “$alice mentioned you in $ROOM”, and you open the app to read it. Answers from b say “Tap to read the answer”. If you turn previews on, the message text goes into the notification so you can read it on your lock screen.

## What we can’t avoid

We want to be exact here, because “our own server” can sound like more than it is.

Phones only accept notifications through their maker’s service. An iPhone notification has to go through Apple’s push service, and an Android one through Google’s Firebase Cloud Messaging. There is no way around that for an app on those phones. So Apple or Google carries the notification to your device, and sees what is in it. That is why previews are off by default: with them off, all Apple or Google can see is that $alice sent you a message, not what she said.

In the web wallet and the extension, notifications use standard Web Push. The browser’s push service carries them, but the content is encrypted for your browser, so the push service can’t read it.

What running our own server changes is the part in the middle. No notification company gets a copy of every user, every device and every conversation. The list of who talks to whom stays with us and bChat, and the stored part is limited to devices and settings.

## What it costs

Apple, Google and the browser push services don’t charge to deliver notifications. The cost is our time and a small server. It runs next to our other services on a server we already rent, and we maintain it ourselves. We had to set up our own Apple push key, a Firebase account and a key pair for Web Push, and those keys live on the server only, never in any code repository.

There are real downsides. When something breaks, nobody else fixes it. Amazon Fire tablets have no Google Play services, so Android push doesn’t reach them. And on an iPhone, the web wallet can only get notifications once it has been added to the home screen. We think that is a fair price for not handing out a map of who our users talk to.

## Turning it on

In the phone apps the switch starts on. In the web wallet and the extension it starts off until you turn it on in Settings, which is when the browser asks for permission. The full details, including how to turn each room down or off, are on the [push notifications page](https://bwalletx.com/push-notifications).

Related: [021 Coordinate on BSV](https://bwalletx.com/blog/021-coordinate-on-bsv) · [024 Pay the person who wrote it](https://bwalletx.com/blog/024-tips-and-paid-likes) · [Chat](https://bwalletx.com/chat) · [Privacy](https://bwalletx.com/privacy)

[← 024 Pay the person who wrote it](https://bwalletx.com/blog/024-tips-and-paid-likes)[026 Paying to be heard →](https://bwalletx.com/blog/026-paying-to-be-heard)

---

Source: https://bwalletx.com/blog/026-paying-to-be-heard

[Development blog](https://bwalletx.com/blog) · 026 · 8 Oct 2026

# Paying to be heard

Priced token rooms in bWalletX: each message burns tokens or pays the issuer, in one transaction. The wallet signs, the server checks before anything is spent. Admins exempt, 50-sat minimum.

Status: live on the server. Priced rooms are enforced by bChat’s server now. The wallet support (paying when you post) is built and will be in the next bWalletX release. This is part 2 of the chat series, after [021 Coordinate on BSV](https://bwalletx.com/blog/021-coordinate-on-bsv).

## The problem with free rooms

A token room in bWalletX is a room only the token’s holders can enter. That already keeps most strangers out. But holding a token is a one-off: once you’re in, every message is free. A room that matters to people attracts the same things a busy group chat does. Someone posts thirty lines in a minute. A small group decides to bury a thread. A bot finds the door and starts talking.

Moderation helps, but it always comes after the damage. We wanted something that changes the maths before anyone types: if every message costs a little, posting thirty lines costs thirty times as much as posting one. A pile-on needs everyone in it to pay. Most people in a room post a few times a day and barely notice the cost. The people who flood a room notice it straight away.

Issuers already had a price-per-message setting in room settings. Until now it was a label. The server didn’t check it. This change makes it real.

## What an issuer can set

The issuer of a token, or an admin of its room, can set a charge per message. There are three kinds:

- Tokens, burned. Each message burns some of the room’s token. Nobody receives it: it is gone from the supply.

- Tokens, to the issuer. Each message sends some of the token to the issuer.

- Sats, to the issuer. Each message pays the issuer in BSV. The minimum is 50 sats.

Why a 50-sat floor? A payment smaller than that costs more in network fees and index work than it is worth. It would make every message more expensive to process without making flooding any more expensive. A token charge has to be at least one unit of the token.

Per-message rules are enforced now. Rooms can also set rules per minute, per hour or per day, and the settings screen says plainly that those aren’t enforced yet.

## One transaction, not two

The obvious way to build this is two steps: pay, then post. That has an ugly failure. You pay, then the post is refused (you sold the token a second ago, the room changed its price, the server was down), and now you have paid for nothing. Or the reverse: the post goes through and the payment doesn’t.

So a priced message is a single Bitcoin transaction with two parts. One part is the payment: the burn, the token transfer or the sats to the issuer. The other is a small record that says which room it is for, who wrote it, a fingerprint (a SHA-256 hash) of the message text, and which version of the room’s rule it was paying. The payment and the message can’t be separated, because they are the same transaction.

## The wallet signs, the server checks, then it is spent

This is the decision we spent most time on. When you post in a priced room, bWalletX builds that transaction and signs it, but it does not broadcast it. It sends the signed transaction to bChat’s server along with your message.

The server then checks everything: that you are a member, that the text matches the fingerprint, that the payment matches the room’s current rule, and that the amounts and the destination are right. Only if all of that passes does the server broadcast the transaction and then store your message.

If the server refuses, it broadcasts nothing. The wallet then cancels the signed transaction and frees the coins it would have used. You can’t end up paid-but-refused. If the network drops halfway, a retry sends the same signed transaction again rather than paying twice.

The wallet also counts a message towards your spending only after the server has accepted it, so a refused message doesn’t eat into your limits.

## You see the price before you pay

Nothing is charged silently. Before you send in a priced room, the wallet shows a line such as “This message costs 5 $ACME, burned” or “This message costs 100 sats to the issuer”. (Those are examples, not real room prices.) You can tell it not to ask again in that room up to an amount you choose, and there is a cap per session, so a long conversation can’t quietly run up a bill.

## Admins don’t pay

The issuer and the room’s admins are exempt. They are the people answering questions, pinning things and keeping the room in order, and charging them to do that would just tax moderation. Everyone else pays the same rule.

## Burned or paid to the issuer?

That is the issuer’s choice. Burning means nobody profits from your message: it just costs you something, which is all the anti-flood effect needs. Paying the issuer means the person who runs the room is paid for the attention. Some rooms will want one, some the other. We show which one applies on every send, so you know where your money goes.

## What we didn’t do

We didn’t take a cut. The charge goes where the issuer set it: burned, or to the issuer. bWalletX adds nothing on top of the normal network fee.

We didn’t make free rooms rarer. Most rooms will stay free. A price is a tool for rooms that need it, not a default.

And we didn’t put token rooms in the store edition. bWallet, on the App Store and Google Play, has no token rooms, so it has no priced rooms either.

## What’s next

Update, 8 Oct 2026: the wallet half shipped in [5.1.85](https://bwalletx.com/releases#v5.1.85), and paid calls by the second arrived with [bPhone](https://bwalletx.com/bphone) in 5.1.87. Still to come: enforcing the per-minute, per-hour and per-day rules, paying for streams by the second, and letting people set their own price to be messaged by strangers. Those are marked Coming on the [Chat page](https://bwalletx.com/chat).

Update, 15 Oct 2026: paying by the minute arrived in Spaces (paid listening, 5.1.95), music pays by the second on bWalletX Desktop (5.2.14), and bMail lets you set your own price to be reached. Still not built: enforcing per-minute, per-hour and per-day message limits in token rooms. The current release is [5.2.24](https://bwalletx.com/releases#v5.2.24).

Source: https://bwalletx.com/blog/027-airdrops-not-dividends

[Development blog](https://bwalletx.com/blog) · 027 · 8 Oct 2026

# Airdrops, not dividends

Why bWalletX issuers reward holders with airdrops, not payouts: the returns-wording block, the airdrop inbox, and the security audit behind it (sandboxed NFT content, address poisoning).

Status: built, not released. The airdrop inbox, the airdrop address, the returns-wording filter and the safety changes below are built on a development branch. They are not in the released app (5.1.84) and will ship in a later release.

Update, 15 Oct 2026: all of this shipped in [5.1.85](https://bwalletx.com/releases#v5.1.85) and is in the current release, 5.2.24. Sending airdrops to holders, followers or room members is still not built, and airdrops that unlock over time wait on token locking, which is in development.

## How do you thank the people who hold your token?

Anyone who launches a token in bWalletX runs into the same question sooner or later: the people holding it backed you early, so how do you thank them? The answer much of crypto reaches for is a share of the money: a cut of fees, a payout per token, “holders earn”. It sounds generous. It is also, in most places, the description of a security. A token that pays holders a share of income looks like a share. Shares are regulated, and selling them to the public without the paperwork is a serious problem for the issuer and for the app that helped.

So we picked a different answer and built the wallet around it: issuers reward holders with airdrops. An airdrop is a gift of tokens or NFTs sent to holders’ wallets. It promises nothing about the future. It is a thing you send, once, that people can keep, use or ignore.

## What a token gives you by default

By default, holding a token in bWalletX gives you one thing: entry to that token’s room. That is the only right we describe. If an issuer says their token does more, the wallet shows it as “Issuer says: …” and marks it as not checked by bWalletX. We don’t verify it and we don’t repeat it as our own claim.

## The returns-wording block

Most people who write “holders get a share of the profits” aren’t trying to sell securities. They are being enthusiastic. So the wallet helps them before it’s a problem.

When you create a token in bWalletX, the wallet watches the name and description as you type. Words like profit, returns, dividends, yield, APY, ROI, “passive income” and “to the moon” bring up a warning, and the wallet won’t sign while they are there: “Remove wording that promises returns before publishing. Describe airdrops or room access instead.”

It matches whole words and ignores obvious look-alikes such as “free returns” or “profit and loss”. It is a word filter, not legal review. Someone determined can get round it. But it catches the common, careless case, and it points people at the answer we want them to use.

## Your airdrop address

Every bWalletX account already has an ordinals address: the address that holds your tokens and NFTs. That is your airdrop address. Receive now has two tabs, Payments and Airdrops, and the Airdrops tab shows that address with a QR code and a copy button. The plan is to show it on your public page as well, so issuers can find it.

## The airdrop inbox

If issuers are going to send people things, people need a calm place to receive them. Otherwise every stranger’s token lands in the middle of your wallet. So anything that turns up unasked goes to an inbox.

The rule for “unasked” is strict: a token or NFT paid to one of your addresses by a transaction you didn’t fund and didn’t start. Anything you bought, minted, launched, swapped or recovered leaves a record in your wallet, so it never counts as an airdrop.

A badge on the Wallet’s Airdrops row counts what is new since you last looked. Each item has two buttons. Keep marks it reviewed; it already shows in your normal tokens or NFTs. Hide removes it, and hides everything else from the same issuer. There is also a switch to show airdrops only from issuers you have kept something from before.

We thought about putting the inbox behind the b button at the top of the screen, so it is visible from every tab. We kept the b where it is and put the badge in the Wallet instead. Airdrops are occasional, and the inbox is new. If people come to rely on it daily, we’ll move it.

## The security audit

An airdrop is, by definition, something a stranger chose to put in your wallet. Before building an inbox that invites people to look at them, we went through every place the wallet displays inscription content and asked what a hostile one could do.

Malicious NFT content is sandboxed. An NFT can be an HTML page or an SVG with script in it. If the wallet rendered that as part of itself, the script would run with the wallet’s access. It never does. Images are shown as images. Anything that isn’t a plain image shows a “tap to preview” placeholder, and the preview opens in a frame with an empty sandbox on a separate origin: no scripts, and no access to the wallet. The audit found two places to tighten. One inherited component used a sandbox setting that was looser than it looked, and the thumbnail code turned SVGs into wallet-origin images. Both are fixed, with a test.

Address poisoning. This scam is common on every chain. Someone sends you a tiny payment, or a worthless token, from an address that looks like one you really pay: the same first four and last four characters. Weeks later you copy an address from your history and pick theirs by mistake. Now, when you type a recipient, the wallet checks it against addresses that sent you dust or unsolicited tokens. If it matches or looks alike, and you’ve never sent to it, you get a warning showing the address it resembles.

No links from the inbox. A token’s name and picture can say anything, including “claim your reward at this site”. The inbox never shows issuer links. Links only appear on a token’s own page, behind a confirmation. The standing rule is printed in the inbox: never type your 12 words on a site an airdrop points to.

## What comes later

Sending airdrops is next: to the followers of an account, to the holders of a token, or to the members of a room, with limits so they can’t be used for spam. Later, airdrops that unlock over time. We have also proposed retiring a TokenBlaster launch option that would pay BSV to holders, which looks too much like a dividend, and replacing it with holder airdrops. No coin uses that option today. Everything we know about the plan is on the [Airdrops page](https://bwalletx.com/airdrops).

[← 026 Paying to be heard](https://bwalletx.com/blog/026-paying-to-be-heard)[028 Launch something with your coin →](https://bwalletx.com/blog/028-launch-something)

---

Source: https://bwalletx.com/blog/028-launch-something

[Development blog](https://bwalletx.com/blog) · 028 · 8 Oct 2026

# Launch something with your coin

A coin should launch with something: token links for website, app, X, Telegram and bChat; the room as the default right; “Issuer says” for the rest; no company field; advanced launch options as plans.

Status: partly built. Buying and selling Launchpad coins is live (since 5.1.74). The Launch your own coin button and token links shipped in [5.1.85](https://bwalletx.com/releases#v5.1.85) (8 Oct 2026). The advanced options at the end are plans.

## A coin with nothing behind it

The Launchpad in bWalletX lists bonding-curve coins made on TokenBlaster. Anyone can launch one in a minute: a ticker, a name, a picture. That is the appeal and the problem. A coin with nothing behind it is a number that goes up and down. People buy it, the price moves, and the conversation is entirely about the price.

We want something different from the Launchpad. A coin should come with something people can use: a website, an app or a product, and somewhere to talk. The owner’s brief was short: “Launch your own coin” is the point, and the coin should launch with something.

## The launch button

Since 5.1.85 there is a full-width gold button at the top of the Launchpad: Launch your own coin. It opens TokenBlaster’s launch page inside the wallet’s browser, with your wallet already connected. On the web wallet and the extension it opens a new tab. The store edition, bWallet, has no Launchpad, so it has no button either.

## Token links

Token pages in bWalletX (on the Exchange, on the Launchpad and in your Wallet) get room for a coin’s links, shown as chips: website, app, X, Telegram and bChat. Each chip shows the domain it goes to.

Links are a way in for scammers, so they are strict. A link must be https with a real hostname, an X link must be on X and a Telegram link on Telegram. Tapping a chip shows a warning first: this is an outside site, not checked by us, and you should never enter your recovery phrase there.

There is one honest catch. Today, no source publishes these links. Token deploy records don’t have the fields, TokenBlaster’s launch form doesn’t ask for them, and neither does the 1Sat index. The wallet reads them as soon as any of those sources does, and shows nothing until then. Adding them to TokenBlaster’s form, signed by the creator, is the next step. Longer term we have proposed a small on-chain “token profile” that only the issuer can sign, so any wallet or market can read it.

Should links be required? We decided not, at first. A coin can launch without them, and the plan is that coins with them rank higher on the board.

## The room is the default right

Here is the decision underneath all of this. When someone buys a coin, what do they get? In bWalletX the answer is one thing, by default: entry to the coin’s room. Every token page says “Holders can enter the $X room”, and the room is the one place every coin has, whatever else it does or doesn’t do.

Anything else is the issuer’s business. If an issuer wants to say their coin gets you a discount, early access or a vote, the wallet shows it as a single line, “Issuer says: …”, with the note “not checked by bWalletX”. It is capped at 160 characters and stripped of anything that could disguise it. We don’t verify it, endorse it or rewrite it as our own claim. That keeps us honest about what we know, and keeps the issuer responsible for what they promise.

## No company field

The most-requested field we left out is “company”: let an issuer say this coin is their business. We said no. A token that stands for a company is a share, and shares are regulated. bChat tried rules for this before, and they got more complicated every week. So token pages never read or show company, equity or share fields, even if a token carries them.

The same goes for wording. When you create a token in bWalletX, the wallet won’t sign a description that promises returns, profits or dividends. If you want to reward your holders, send them an airdrop: see [027 Airdrops, not dividends](https://bwalletx.com/blog/027-airdrops-not-dividends).

Company tokens may come one day, but as a separate product with identity checks, never as a field on ordinary coins.

## Advanced options: plans

Today every TokenBlaster coin launches on the same curve with the same settings. We have written up a set of advanced options for the launch form. None of this is built. It would be built in TokenBlaster, behind a collapsed Advanced panel, with the one-tap standard launch staying first.

- Curve presets. A few named shapes (Standard, Gentle, Steep, Late graduation) instead of free-form numbers, with bounds so no preset can trap buyers. The wallet’s own trade check has to read each coin’s curve before any of these can launch.

- Fee mix. Splitting the creator’s share of fees between the creator, a group of wallets and buybacks, fixed at launch.

- Buybacks. Part of each fee buys the coin and burns it, with limits on how often and how much one buy can move the price.

- Tranches. Releasing supply on a schedule instead of all at once, using the same curve shapes as [Lock BSV](https://bwalletx.com/lock), with a preview chart and each tranche time-locked on chain once token locks are proven to index correctly.

- Milestones. Releases tied to events, such as the coin graduating from its curve or witnesses confirming that an app shipped, each with a deadline after which the tranche releases or burns, as the issuer chose at launch.

We describe all of these as a supply schedule or a fee setting, never as rewards. A buyback isn’t a promise about the price, and a tranche isn’t a promise of anything.

## Where to start

Open Exchange in bWalletX and tap the Launchpad bar to trade coins today. The full picture, with what is live and what is coming, is on the [Launchpad page](https://bwalletx.com/launchpad).

[← 027 Airdrops, not dividends](https://bwalletx.com/blog/027-airdrops-not-dividends)[029 bPositive: gifts, not investments →](https://bwalletx.com/blog/029-bpositive)

Source: https://bwalletx.com/blog/029-bpositive

[Development blog](https://bwalletx.com/blog) · 029 · 8 Oct 2026

# bPositive: gifts, not investments

bPositive lets you sponsor someone’s journey in bWalletX: monthly support, witness-confirmed milestone pledges, thank-you NFTs. Why it is gifts only, and the decisions behind it.

Status: plan, with the owner’s decisions made (8 Oct 2026). No bPositive code exists yet. Everything below is Coming.

Update, 15 Oct 2026: still a plan. No bPositive code exists, and nothing below is in the current release (5.2.24). To go live it needs journey records, pledges held in pots, witness confirmation with verified identities, and thank-you NFTs, all built and tested.

## Backing a person, not a coin

A lot of what happens around a wallet is about tokens and prices. bPositive is about people. It lets you back someone who is working towards something: a student saving for an exam, an athlete training for a race, someone in recovery counting days, a developer learning a new stack, an artist finishing an album.

People already do this informally. A friend sends money every month. A relative promises a sum if you pass. The trouble is that the promise lives in someone’s head, the proof is “trust me”, and strangers who would like to help have no way in. bPositive puts the money, the proof and the people in one place, which is bWalletX.

## Gifts, not investments

The first rule, before any screen was drawn: sponsoring is a gift. A sponsor gets no returns, no share of future earnings, no equity and no repayment.

We could have built the other thing. “Back a young developer, get 2% of what they earn” is an obvious pitch. It is also an income-share agreement, which in many places is a regulated financial product. It puts pressure on the person in exactly the wrong way: their success becomes someone else’s return. And it pulls in the people who want a return rather than the people who want to help.

So there is nothing to get back. The single exception is your own money that was never released: if you pledge to a milestone and it isn’t confirmed by the deadline, the pledge comes back to you. That is not a return. It is a gift that didn’t happen.

For the same reason there is no bPositive token. A token would muddy the rule straight away. And bPositive will never be combined with a launchpad coin on the same journey. It is the same thinking as [027 Airdrops, not dividends](https://bwalletx.com/blog/027-airdrops-not-dividends).

## Three building blocks

bPositive is mostly made of parts bWalletX already has.

Monthly support uses pots. “Support monthly” is a standing order from one of your pots to the person’s paymail, tagged to their journey. You can pause or cancel it any time. A gift that has been paid is final, but nothing more goes out once you stop.

Milestones use witnesses. The person names a milestone (“Pass the AWS Associate exam”, “Run a sub-4 marathon”, “90 days sober”), what will count as evidence, and a deadline. They choose witnesses, and each witness has to accept. When the person says they’ve done it, witnesses confirm or decline with a signed seal recorded on chain. By default 2 of 3 must confirm.

Recognition uses NFTs. Sponsors get a thank-you receipt NFT. Later, the person gets an achievement badge when a milestone is confirmed. Neither unlocks anything in the app, and neither has any promised value.

## A pledge before a lock

The hardest design question was how to hold a milestone pledge. The strong version is an on-chain lock: a script that can pay the person only when witnesses sign, and can pay the sponsor back only after the deadline. Nobody, including us, could move the money any other way. It is also new script code, and new script code holding other people’s money needs testing and an independent review before it goes anywhere near mainnet.

So we are doing it in two steps, and saying so. In the first version a pledge stays in a pot in the sponsor’s own wallet. When the witnesses confirm, the sponsor’s wallet sends it the next time it is open. That is a promise, not a lock: the sponsor could cancel, and the money waits for their wallet. The app labels it honestly as “Pledged (paid when confirmed, from the sponsor’s wallet)”, never as locked.

The second version is the real lock, with the release pinned to the person’s own key. Even the person plus all the witnesses couldn’t send it anywhere else. Refunds after the deadline happen automatically when the sponsor next opens the wallet.

## Witnesses need to be real

The obvious abuse is a fake milestone confirmed by friends. Witnesses need a verified identity, are shown publicly on the journey page with their identity strength, and can’t be the person’s other accounts or a sponsor of the same milestone. Larger amounts need stronger identities. Witnesses are not paid for witnessing: a fee for saying yes is the wrong incentive. Sponsors see who the witnesses are before they pledge, and decide for themselves.

## The other decisions

- 18+ at launch. Recipients, witnesses and milestone sponsors must be adults. Journeys for younger people raise problems we’d rather solve properly later than badly now.

- 0% fee. The Bitcoin Corporation takes nothing from gifts, as with tips in bChat. You pay the normal network fee.

- Sponsor count, not totals. Journey pages show how many people sponsor. Showing amounts is the person’s choice. No countdowns, no leaderboards: those reward urgency, which is what scams use.

- Sponsors’ rooms are opt-in. The person can open a room for sponsors who hold a thank-you NFT. Sponsoring gives no right to contact the person, and they can block a sponsor.

- Not in the store edition at first. A public page with a goal and a list of sponsors looks like fundraising to App Store and Google Play reviewers, which brings its own rules. bWallet, the store edition, keeps ordinary person-to-person payments and standing orders, and bPositive lives in bWalletX.

## What happens next

The first phase is journey pages, monthly support and thank-you NFTs, with pledges labelled as pledges. Witness-confirmed milestones with the on-chain lock come second, after the script has been tested and reviewed. The rules as they stand are on the [bPositive page](https://bwalletx.com/bpositive).

Only give what you would give a friend. Gifts can have tax consequences where you live; we can’t advise on them.

[← 028 Launch something with your coin](https://bwalletx.com/blog/028-launch-something)[030 bPhone: charge to receive calls →](https://bwalletx.com/blog/030-bphone)

Source: https://bwalletx.com/blog/030-bphone

[Development blog](https://bwalletx.com/blog) · 030 · 8 Oct 2026

# bPhone: charge to receive calls

Calls in bWalletX have always been free. From 5.1.87 you can put a price on yours: per second, minute, hour or call, in BSV, MNEE or a token, paid from the caller’s wallet to yours while you are still talking. This is how it works, and why it is built the way it is.

Status: live since [5.1.87](https://bwalletx.com/releases#v5.1.87) (8 Oct 2026), in bWalletX, not the store edition. It is new: start with small prices.

## Whose time is the product

A therapist, a solicitor, an accountant in January, a developer who will look at your broken deploy, a language tutor, someone who has been where you are. All of them sell time, and today most of them sell it through a platform that sits in the middle: it takes 15 to 30 percent, holds the money for a week or a month, decides when to pay out, and keeps the client list. The call itself goes through the platform too, so leaving it means losing the clients.

bWalletX already has the pieces that platform provides. Calls run on our own video server. Names resolve to identity keys. Payments go wallet to wallet in under a second. The missing piece was small: a published price, and a meter.

## The rate card

Under Chat › Calls there is a new bPhone tab. You turn on “Charge to receive calls” and pick three things: the asset, the amount and the unit. The asset is dollars paid in BSV, MNEE, or any BSV-21 token you hold. The unit is a second, a minute, an hour, or the whole call. That is the whole rate card:

``{ amount: 2, per: 'minute', asset: { kind: 'bsv' } }``

It is published under your identity key on the paymail server, signed the same way your paymail claim is, so anyone who is about to call you can read it first. Your phone keeps a copy, because it is the side that has to enforce it.

BSV prices are in dollars. That is the rule we set for streams last week and it holds here: you say “$2 a minute”, the caller’s wallet turns each payment into satoshis at the live rate. MNEE is a dollar already. A token price is in tokens, which means a $NAME token finally has something its holders can spend it on: a call with you.

## Nothing rings until the caller agrees

When someone dials you, their wallet fetches your card before it places the call. If there is one, they see it: the rate, “paid every 10 seconds from your wallet while you talk”, and three choices for the most they are willing to spend, worked out as 15, 30 and 60 minutes at your rate. Accept, and the call rings. Cancel, and nothing happened. There is no way to reach the ringing state without passing the quote.

We thought about charging from the moment of ringing, so a callee’s time waiting for you to pick up is paid. We decided against it: a missed call that cost money is the kind of thing that makes people stop using a feature. The meter starts when the callee answers.

## The meter

The caller’s phone runs the meter. Every 10 seconds in BSV, every 60 in MNEE or a token (each of those transfers pays an indexing fee, so they are batched longer), it sends one ordinary payment to the callee: a paymail payment for BSV, a transfer to the address in the card for the others. It pays one interval ahead, five seconds before the paid time runs out, so the callee is never owed money and the caller’s exposure if the callee hangs up is one interval.

Rounding was the part we got wrong first. $2 a minute is 33.3 cents per 10 seconds; round that up every time and an hour costs $122.40 instead of $120. The meter now charges exactly what the rate says is owed through the new paid-until time, minus what has been paid: 34 cents, then 33, then 33, and so on. Over any length of call the total is the rate, to the cent.

After each payment the caller’s phone sends a small receipt to the callee over the call’s own data channel: a sequence number, the amount, the time it pays through, the transaction id. The callee’s screen shows “Received $4.20 · paid 7 s ahead”. The caller’s shows “Spent $4.20 of $60”, and a warning 30 seconds before the maximum. When the call ends, both see the total.

## The callee enforces it

The callee’s phone trusts nobody. If the first receipt has not arrived within 20 seconds of answering, it hangs up. After that, if the paid-through time is more than 10 seconds in the past, it hangs up, with “Ended: not paid” on the screen. A caller on an older build, or on the store edition, never sees the quote and never pays, so they get about 20 seconds and are cut off. That is the intended behaviour: a callee who set a price should not be giving free calls to people whose app is out of date.

What the callee’s phone does not yet do is check the chain for each transaction id during the call. The paymail server already verifies that every BSV payment it receives pays the exact outputs it handed out, and the wallet collects those payments as it always has, so a forged receipt buys a caller at most one grace period before the inbox shows nothing arrived. A server-side ledger that matches receipts to transactions during the call is the obvious next step, and we have written down where it goes.

Update, 15 Oct 2026: bPhone shipped in [5.1.87](https://bwalletx.com/releases#v5.1.87). The per-transaction chain check during a call described above is still not built.

## The directory and bookings

Charging and being found are separate switches. You can charge without being listed, so only people who already know your name pay for your time. Or you can list yourself: a title, a few lines about what you offer, a category, and opening hours in your own time zone. The listing appears under Chat › Calls › Experts for everyone, with your rate and whether you are open right now. Outside your hours you can still be called; the directory just says “Opens Thu 09:00”.

Bookings came out of the same conversation. Someone who wants an hour of your time next Tuesday should not have to catch you free. They pick a slot inside your hours, 15 to 60 minutes, and you confirm it or decline. From five minutes before the start a Call now button appears on both phones. The booked call is a normal bPhone call, quoted and paid the same way; there is no deposit and no charge for a no-show in this version. We would rather see how people use it first.

## No middle, 0%

The Bitcoin Corporation takes nothing from a bPhone call, as with tips and with gifts. There is no platform balance anywhere: every payment is from the caller’s wallet to the callee’s, and the only server involved stores the published price and the bookings. If we disappeared tomorrow, the people in your call history would still be callable and payable by name.

There are no refunds either. A payment is a payment. The maximum the caller sets is the most a call can cost, and the grace period is the most a callee can be short. Both are small on purpose.

## What is still to do

- Apply the database change on the paymail server and ship the wallet build, then test with real money: BSV, MNEE, a token, a flat price, an old build calling a priced callee, the cap, an empty wallet.

- A receipt ledger on the server, so “received” on the callee’s screen means “verified”.

- Push ringing, so a booked call rings a phone with the app closed. Calls still ring only while the app is open.

- Booking reminders, and a calendar export.

- Not in the store edition until the rules on person-to-person services are settled with a reviewer.

The rules as they stand, and a worked table of what a call costs, are on the [bPhone page](https://bwalletx.com/bphone).

You are selling your time to people you may not know. Any licence, confidentiality or tax rule that applies to your profession applies here too; bPhone checks none of it, and says so.

# bWalletX 5.1.88: a new Calls tab, working mics, a new menu

bWalletX 5.1.88 shipped on 8 Oct 2026. It is on the App Store (build 82), on Play (build 76), at web.bwalletx.com, in the Chrome extension and as a direct APK. Most of it is about talking to people: a proper Calls tab, microphones that work, and a menu that handles more than one account.

The full list is in the [5.1.88 release notes](https://bwalletx.com/releases?v=5.1.88#v5.1.88). This is the short version.

## A Calls tab

Calls now has four tabs: Recents, Contacts, Services and a green Keypad. Recents is who you called and who called you. Contacts is the people you know by name. Services is the list of people who charge for their time. Keypad lets you dial a $handle or a paymail directly.

At the top sits a yellow bPhone card. That is where you set a price to receive calls, if you want one. How the price and the meter work is on the [bPhone page](https://bwalletx.com/bphone).

## Microphones and cameras that work

In earlier builds the mic or camera could fail to start in Spaces and in calls. That is fixed. You now see sound bars next to whoever is talking, so you can tell your mic is live without asking.

The Chrome extension needs one more step, because Chrome only asks for mic permission from a normal tab. The extension now opens a small tab that asks once. After that, calls and Spaces work from the side panel.

## A new menu

The account menu was rebuilt. It shows up to four accounts inline, so switching is one tap. Below them: All accounts, Agents, Settings, and Sign out with a lock. If you run an agent account next to your own, it sits in the same place.

You can also sign out of chat for one account without touching the others.

## Identity

There is a new Identity map screen. It shows the names, accounts and keys tied to your wallet, and how they connect. Your wallet card now has a line under the name saying which identity it is. The [Identity map page](https://bwalletx.com/identity-map) explains what each part means.

When your account signs in somewhere new, the wallet now alerts you. Settings has a Recent sign-ins list, so you can see where and when.

## Rooms and Spaces

- Invite links for Spaces and rooms. Send one and the person lands in the right place.

- A room history option, for chat rooms only: choose whether new members can read what was said before they joined.

- A private welcome in the Lounge, so a new account gets a short hello that only they can see.

More on Spaces is on the [bSpaces page](https://bwalletx.com/bspaces).

## The web wallet

The web wallet layout now matches the app. Same tabs, same menu, same places for things. If you use both, you no longer have to remember two layouts.

Source: https://bwalletx.com/blog/032-meet-bchatx

[Development blog](https://bwalletx.com/blog) · 032 · 8 Oct 2026

# Meet bChatX.com

Chat has a new home: [www.bchatx.com](https://chat.bwalletx.com). It is the same chat you know from bWalletX, built for the web, and it looks like the wallet.

## It looks like bWalletX

bChatX uses the bWalletX colours: dark, with yellow only where it matters, such as the button you are meant to press. Along the bottom is the same kind of bar as the app: Feed, Rooms, b, Spaces and DMs.

In the top bar is a wallet chip. If you are signed in it shows your $handle with a dot. If you are not, it says Get bWalletX.

## Your wallet is bWalletX

bChatX does not make you a second wallet. Your wallet is bWalletX. When you do something with money, such as a tip, a paid like or joining a token room, bChatX opens bWalletX and the wallet asks you to approve it. Your keys stay there.

That is also why sign-in starts with Sign in with bWalletX. Google and LinkedIn are still there, under More ways, but they don’t give you a wallet. You can read and post, and when you want to pay someone you will need bWalletX anyway.

## A faster feed

The feed used to load after the page, so you watched it fill in. Now the posts arrive with the page itself. On a normal connection that is about half a second from opening the link to reading.

## Safety in the feed

The feed shows posts from other BSV apps as well as bChat. That brings in things we don’t control, so there are new switches:

- Show Twetch posts. A switch to hide or show them. Twetch stays in All by default.

- Language. On posts from other apps, slurs are hidden and swearing is masked.

- Images. Images from other apps are blurred until you tap them.

- Report. Every post has a report button.

Nothing is deleted from the chain. These are choices about what bChatX shows you.

## The other addresses

bitcoinchat.online and bit-sign.online will point to bChatX over time. If you have bookmarks there, they will keep working and lead to the same place.

[← 031 bWalletX 5.1.88](https://bwalletx.com/blog/031-calls-mics-menu)[033 Spaces you can just listen to →](https://bwalletx.com/blog/033-spaces-you-can-listen-to)

[Development blog](https://bwalletx.com/blog) · 033 · 8 Oct 2026

# Spaces you can just listen to

Spaces are live audio rooms: a few people talk, everyone else listens. They now have their own page at [www.bchatx.com/spaces](https://chat.bwalletx.com/spaces), and you can listen to a public one without signing in.

## The Spaces page

The page has three parts.

- Live now. Each Space shows the host, how many speakers and listeners, and a Listen button.

- Recent. Spaces that have ended. Each one keeps a page, so a link shared yesterday still goes somewhere.

- Start a Space. Open your own.

## Listen without signing in

For a public Space, you tap Listen and you are in. No account, no wallet. You can only listen.

When you want to do more, such as raise your hand to speak, react or tip a speaker, bChatX asks you to sign in. Tipping uses your bWalletX, as with everything that involves money.

Some Spaces are for holders of a token. Those still need sign-in, because the server has to check you hold it. Private rooms are never listed on the page at all.

## The stage

A Space can have up to 12 speakers on stage at once. Everyone else is a listener until the host brings them up.

## Strict networks

Audio goes directly between devices where it can. Some networks block that: offices, hotels, some mobile carriers. We have added a TURN relay, which carries the audio through our server when a direct path fails. People on those networks can now join.

## Coming: Game Spaces

Game Spaces are coming: watch TokenBlaster matches live, with the players talking. More when it is ready.

Update, 15 Oct 2026: Game Spaces are not built yet. Since this post, Spaces gained pay at the door, paid listening and Broadcast (share a tab or screen) in bWalletX.

The [bSpaces page](https://bwalletx.com/bspaces) has more on how Spaces work inside bWalletX.

Source: https://bwalletx.com/blog/034-open-apps-open-protocol

[Development blog](https://bwalletx.com/blog) · 034 · 8 Oct 2026

# Open apps, open protocol

If chat on BSV is going to compete with Telegram, people have to be able to trust it, and other developers have to be able to build on it. Both are easier when the code is open. This is how we are doing it, and what stays closed for now.

## Why open matters for chat

Chat is where people say things they would not post publicly. You should be able to check what the app does with your messages and your keys, or ask someone you trust to check. And a chat network only gets big if more than one company can write apps for it. A protocol nobody else can read is a walled garden with extra steps.

## The model

Three parts: open-source apps, an open protocol, and a server that stays closed for now.

## Open-source apps

bWalletX is already open source under the MIT licence. bChat desktop and the bChatX web app will follow under the same licence. MIT means you can read the code, change it, and ship your own version.

The names and logos are trademarks. You can fork the code, but your fork needs its own name.

## An open protocol

The bChat Protocol is public on GitHub at [github.com/bitcoin-corp/bchat-protocol](https://github.com/bitcoin-corp/bchat-protocol). It describes how messages, rooms and payments are written to the chain, so another app can read and write the same things.

Alongside it is the bChatX Protocol proposal, for threads that work across apps: a reply in Twetch, Treechat or peck.to showing up under the post it replies to, wherever that post was made. It is a proposal, not a finished standard. peck.to already threads bChat replies.

## Why the server stays closed for now

The server does moderation, anti-spam and the paid features. Publishing the anti-spam rules mostly helps spammers, and the moderation tools are still changing week to week. So the server is closed for now.

What matters is what the server can’t do. Your keys never leave your wallet. The server can’t spend your money. Every payment is signed in your wallet, by you.

More on what is open and where to find it is on the [open source page](https://bwalletx.com/open-source).

# Pots & Locks, and backing PNEEs

Locking BSV until a date, or paying it out to yourself over time, has been in bWalletX since 5.1.84. Today the Lock screen becomes Pots & Locks, so your locks are grouped by what they are for.

## What changed

The screen opens with two buttons, Lock BSV and + Pot, and one total for everything in your pots, with Claim when a payout is ready.

Below that, your locks are grouped into pots. A lock started from a template, such as Pension, Savings goal, Holiday fund or Rainy-day fund, goes into that pot. Locks you made before pots existed sit under Other locks. Tap a pot to see its locks and add another.

With no locks yet, you see a Start a pot card with the templates, so you can begin from a goal rather than a blank form.

## Nothing taken away

Every lock feature stays: one unlock date or payouts over time, the payout curves, templates, claim, re-lock, receipts and the public check at [bwalletx.com/lock/verify](https://bwalletx.com/lock/verify). A lock still can’t be broken early, not even by you. The grouping is just a label in your wallet. The coins don’t depend on it.

## Backing PNEEs

PNEEs are our BSV-backed dollar token, in a small pilot since post [011](https://bwalletx.com/blog/011-pnees-pilot). The lock button on the PNEEs card now opens a Back PNEEs card that explains what backing means, then asks how much BSV to lock.

Continue opens the normal lock builder, filled in for you: a lock called “PNEEs backing”, one unlock date a year out, in the PNEEs pot. You review it and type LOCK to confirm, like any other lock. The lock then shows as your PNEEs pot, at the top of Pots & Locks.

## Where it is

Live on [web.bwalletx.com](https://web.bwalletx.com) and the desktop beta at [beta.bwalletx.com](https://beta.bwalletx.com).

# Subscriptions, priced in dollars

A subscription should cost what it says, whatever the BSV price does this month. So subscriptions in bWalletX are priced in dollars and paid in BSV at the day’s rate.

## How a payment works

You approve a subscription once: the service, the dollar amount and how often. Each period, when you open the wallet, it pays that period’s dollar amount in BSV at that day’s rate. The service can only receive the agreed amount, once per period.

Nothing is locked or paid up front. Prepaying a year at today’s price is just paying a year in advance, and it can’t follow the price, so we don’t do it.

## Paid from a pot

Each subscription pays from a pot you choose, such as a Subscriptions pot. Pausing the pot pauses everything paid from it. If a falling BSV price means a pot will run short, the wallet tells you.

## One list

Pots & Locks has a Subscriptions card showing how many are active and about what they cost a month. It opens a list of all your subscriptions, with:

- roughly what each costs a month, and about how much BSV the next payment is today

- which pot pays for it, which you can change

- Pause all and Resume all

You can cancel any time.

## Where it is

Live on [web.bwalletx.com](https://web.bwalletx.com) and the desktop beta at [beta.bwalletx.com](https://beta.bwalletx.com).

[← 035 Pots & Locks, and backing PNEEs](https://bwalletx.com/blog/035-pots-and-locks)[037 Portfolio vs market →](https://bwalletx.com/blog/037-portfolio-vs-market)

[Development blog](https://bwalletx.com/blog) · 037 · 10 Oct 2026

# Portfolio vs market

The price tile at the top left of the wallet used to open the BSV chart. Now it opens Portfolio vs market: how your wallet is doing, compared with the obvious alternatives.

## What it shows

- what your wallet is worth now, and your gain or loss in dollars and percent over the range you pick

- ranges of 1 day, 1 week, 1 month, 1 year or all time

- a vs market chart: your return against just holding BSV, holding BTC, or keeping dollars, with a line you can drag to read every line at one point

- a value chart in dollars

- your holdings, including locked BSV and MNEE, with each one’s share and change, and your best and worst

- today’s BSV price and change, and a button to the full BSV chart

## How it is worked out

Your BSV on each day, locks included, comes from your own transaction history, priced at that day’s rate. Money you send in or out isn’t counted as a gain or a loss; fees are.

Some figures are estimates, and the screen says so. When it has to use a nearby day’s price, it shows “Estimated”. Tokens are left out of the history line because their past prices aren’t known, and the screen says that too. If prices can’t be loaded, it tells you rather than showing made-up numbers.

## Where it is

Live on [web.bwalletx.com](https://web.bwalletx.com) and the desktop beta at [beta.bwalletx.com](https://beta.bwalletx.com).
