# Swap into BSV

Most people arrive holding something other than BSV. The Swap into BSV card on the bWalletX home screen turns it into BSV in your own wallet.

## How it works

- Pick the coin you have, from a list of 1,000+ with search and the popular ones first.

- Enter an amount and see about how much BSV you get.

- Get a deposit address and send your coin to it from wherever it is now.

- Track it: deposit seen, swapping, sending BSV, in your wallet. You can leave the screen; it carries on.

The swap is run by ChangeNOW, not by bWalletX, and the BSV goes straight to your own wallet address. We never hold your coins. ChangeNOW may pause a swap for checks and ask for details before releasing or refunding it. Rates float, so the amount you get can differ a little from the first quote.

## A permanent card

The swap card used to have an × to hide it, and then there was no way to bring it back. It is now always on the home screen, and anyone who hid it gets it back. There is also a page about it at [bwalletx.com/swap](https://bwalletx.com/swap).

Swaps are in bWalletX, not in the App Store and Google Play edition.

## Where it is

Live on [web.bwalletx.com](https://web.bwalletx.com) and the desktop beta at [beta.bwalletx.com](https://beta.bwalletx.com).

# bGigs: your stage, your fans

Artists can play live to their fans from anywhere, sell tickets at the door or by the minute, and get paid straight away. It works today in bWalletX.

## Your own stage

Every artist gets a Space with a link that never changes. Go live on camera and mic from your phone or the web, bring a guest up on stage, and talk to the room while you play.

It works across the world: the promoter can run the room in London while the artist plays from Tokyo.

## Tickets that pay you

Set a door price and fans pay once to come in. Or charge by the minute, so fans pay only for what they hear and can leave whenever they like.

Either way the money goes straight to the artist, as it comes in. No waiting weeks for a payout.

## Featured artists

[VexVoidEchoes in the Dust · Artist Proof](https://vexvoid.com)
[NPGXTokyo Gutter Punk](https://npgx.website)
[VexVoidEchoes in the Dust · Ultra](https://vexvoid.com)
[NPGXNeon Blood Riot](https://npgx.website)
[VexVoidEchoes in the Dust · Ultra](https://vexvoid.com)
[VexVoidEchoes in the Dust · Rare](https://vexvoid.com)

## What's not done

- Playing your music video into the room, in sync for everyone, on repeat if you like.
- Album Spaces: a ticketed run of your music videos, one after another.
- Your own banner on your Space and tile (in the next app build).
- Splitting ticket money between promoter, label, artist and crew.
- Tickets are in bWalletX (web, Android and Chrome), not the App Store or Google Play editions.

Related: [Home](https://bwalletx.com/) · [Features](https://bwalletx.com/features) · [Developers](https://bwalletx.com/developers)

# Pay artists by the second

Echoes in the Abyss by VexVoid is in bWalletX. The first six tracks are free, the rest cost 1 sat a second, and the money goes straight to the artist.

## One album, twelve tracks

Open Media in bWalletX Desktop and the album is on the front shelf, with a big square cover. Track 1 is free. Tracks 2 to 6 are sponsored: VexVoid pays for your listening from a pot, so you hear them free too.

Tracks 7 to 12 cost 1 sat for each second you listen. Stop when you like and you stop paying. Every sat goes to the artist's wallet as you listen, not weeks later.

## The listener board

Fans can opt in to a board of top listeners, with their rank and badges. It is your choice to join, and you can opt out again at any time.

## For artists

Press "Add a release" in bWalletX Desktop to publish your own music or video with a square cover, on chain. Listeners pay you by the second, and you can sponsor them from a pot so they hear you free.

The new page at bwalletx.com/artists shows the album and how to start.

# NFTs that just work

Sending an NFT is now two steps. NFTs sent to you say who sent them, open in a viewer, and wait for you to keep them. Video NFTs show their cover, and duplicates can be burned.

## Send in two steps

Choose "Who gets it?", then press one Send button. That's all. If a send does fail, the wallet tells you why.

## When someone sends you one

NFTs sent to you show who sent them. Tap one to open it in a viewer. If you want it, press Keep and it moves into your NFTs. If not, leave it where it is.

## Video covers

Video NFTs show their cover art in the list, and they play on iPhone too.

## Burn the duplicates

If you have more copies than you want, open one and choose Burn. You confirm by typing BURN or holding the button for two seconds. If it is your only copy, the wallet warns you first.

# Chats that feel like Telegram

# Ask b

b, the helper inside bWalletX, has a calmer home. Hold the gold b to talk, and your chats on bChatX now have their own links.

## A quiet place to ask

b opens on a dark pool with a few gentle suggestions drifting past: a savings pot, sending money to someone, pocket money. Or just type your own question.

## Hold to talk

Hold the gold b and speak. Your words appear in the box, and nothing sends until you do. b can fill in a payment for you, but nothing goes until you say so.

## Correction, 25 Oct 2026

This post first said your chats with b were “kept private” and encrypted. That was misleading, and we have changed it. b is our team’s assistant: when you talk to b you are talking to us. Each message reaches our server and our AI provider readable, and we read and keep conversations with b for up to 180 days to fix bugs and improve the app. They are not end-to-end encrypted. [What happens to your chats with b](https://bwalletx.com/talk-to-b).

## Your chats with b, with their own links

On bChatX, Ask b lives at bchatx.com/ask-b. Each chat has its own link, so you can come back to it. Pin the ones you use and hide the ones you don't; opening hidden chats asks your wallet to sign first.

With bWalletX connected, the chat list you scroll back through is locked with your wallet, so other people can’t browse it. That does not make the chat private from us: our team can read what you tell b.

# Your token's own page and agent

Every token on bChatX has a full page: price, chart, holders, posts and a Buy button. Its creator can give it an agent, and holders can show a badge name.

## A page for every token

Open a token, like bchatx.com/t/VEXVOID, to see the token's price and chart, its holders, whether its Space is live, its posts and a Buy button. Tap any avatar to see it full screen. The pages also have their own share cards.

## Token agents

A token's creator can give it an agent with a name ending in .agent, like vexvoid.agent. It greets people, welcomes new holders and answers questions about the token in its room, using what was said there recently. It never talks about price.

Names with a dot are reserved for these, so nobody can claim a lookalike.

## Badge names and members

In a token room your name shows with the token beside it, like john.frogger, while you hold it. Holders can choose to appear in the token's members list, and choose who may message them: any holder, only people they've chatted with, or nobody. A first message arrives as a request you can accept.

# Stays unlocked, sends exactly

bWalletX no longer locks itself after a few minutes, and fingerprint unlock on Android works again. Token sends show the exact amount before anything is paid.

## No more surprise locks

Auto-lock now defaults to Never. You can still lock the wallet yourself, or set a timer in Settings if you prefer one.

## Fingerprint on Android

Fingerprint unlock works again on Android. If it ever needs setting up again, the wallet asks you.

## Token sends you can check

Before a token send pays the indexer, you see the exact amount and confirm it. If your wallet is out of date for that token, one tap on "Fix and send" puts it right and sends.

# Pay the artist

bMusic is on bWalletX Desktop. Anyone can open an artist page and hear the first track without signing in. The next tracks are paid for by the artist, and after that your money goes straight to them.

## Artists in bMusic

Open [desktop.bwalletx.com/bmusic/artists](https://desktop.bwalletx.com/bmusic/artists) and pick an artist. VexVoid is first. The artist page has a short bio, every track, a video, the price of the originals, and the people who have listened most.

## Try before you sign up

You don’t need a wallet to look around. Track 1 plays straight away, with no account. If you like it, bWalletX offers to make you a wallet in a minute, and the next few tracks are paid for by the artist’s own pot. You don’t pay for those.

For the rest of the album, bWalletX shows you how to add a little BSV: swap another coin into it, or receive some from a friend. Then you carry on where you left off.

## Paid by the second, paid to the artist

Paid tracks cost 1 sat a second while they play. Stop the track and the payment stops. The money goes from your wallet to the artist. Nobody takes a cut in the middle.

## A Tip button too

The artist page, each track and the album player all have a Tip button. Pick 10p, 50p, £1, £5 or your own amount, then tap Allow once. All of it goes to the artist.

# Your NFTs, edge to edge

bWalletX Desktop has an NFT library. Every picture, clip and song you own is in one grid, opens edge to edge, and a moment from a video can become the art on your card.

## One library

On Desktop, go to Wallet → NFTs ([desktop.bwalletx.com/wallet/nfts](https://desktop.bwalletx.com/wallet/nfts)). Everything you own is in one grid, with a preview for each kind: pictures, video, music and documents. Filter by kind, open a collection, or search. NFTs that are still on their way say so.

Tickets and credits have their own tabs next to it, so the grid is just your things.

## Edge to edge

Open an NFT and the picture or clip fills the space in its own shape. There is no frame around it: the screen is the frame. Video plays where it is, and the details and actions sit around it, not on top of it.

If you’ve just been sent an NFT and it’s still on its way, it plays already, straight from your wallet.

## A frame from a clip, on your card

In the card designer, My NFTs now lists your video clips too. Pick one, slide to the moment you like, and tap Use this frame. That still goes on your card and is kept in My pictures.

## Tip the creator

When an NFT names who made it, its page has a Tip button for them.

# Tip buttons

bWalletX Desktop has a Tip button for artists, NFT creators, rooms, people in chat, friends and speakers in Spaces. Pick an amount, tap Allow once, and all of it goes to them.

## Where you’ll find it

- bMusic: the artist page, each track, and the album player.

- NFTs: the creator, when the NFT names one.

- Chat: the room’s creator in the header, and each person by their name.

- Friends: on each friend’s page.

- Spaces: each speaker on stage.

You never see a Tip button on your own things.

## One sheet, one Allow

Pick 10p, 50p, £1 or £5 (or 10¢, 50¢, $1, $5), or type your own amount, and add a note if you like. bWalletX works out the BSV at today’s price. Tap Allow once.

## All of it goes to them

The tip goes from your wallet to theirs. We take nothing. If the network is slow, the wallet tells you it’s on its way, so you don’t pay twice.

# bRadio: live audio in bWalletX

Host a live audio Space, bring people up to speak, and keep listening while you use the rest of the wallet. Recorded Spaces can become podcast episodes.

## Go live

Start a Space and you’re the host. People join to listen. Anyone can raise a hand, and you bring them up to the stage to speak. Whoever is talking gets a gold ring round their bAvatar, so you always know who’s speaking.

When someone you follow goes live, you get a notification: “$name is hosting”. Tap it and you’re in.

## Keep listening

Leave the Space screen and it keeps playing. A live bar sits at the top and a mini player at the bottom, so you can pay, chat or browse and still hear the room. Tap either one to go back in.

## The bRadio Lounge

The [bRadio Lounge](https://chat.bwalletx.com/r/BRADIO) is the place to find people talking and to try it out. Drop in, listen, raise a hand.

## Podcasts from Spaces

A recorded Space can become a podcast episode. Anyone can play a free preview. This is off by default: nothing is recorded or published unless the host turns it on.

An episode can also be an NFT. Whoever owns it can listen to the whole thing.

# Digital Ice-Cream

A story about three friends, an ice-cream stand and digital cash, and where we’re taking bWalletX next.

Here’s where we’re taking bWalletX. It’s easiest to tell as a story.

## Fred, Joe and You

Fred, Joe and You open an ice-cream stand. Real ice cream, in real cones. Customers pay in digital cash from their phones.

You agree the split up front: Fred 30%, Joe 30%, You 40%. Every sale is split the moment it’s paid. Nobody does the sums at the end of the month, and nobody has to trust whoever holds the till.

## Shares that stay put

Each partner’s share is locked. It takes the partners together to move it, so no one can quietly sell out or hand theirs to a stranger.

## Max joins

Summer gets busy and Max comes in to help, for 10%. Everyone gives up a little: the split becomes Fred 27%, Joe 27%, You 36%, Max 10%. The partners agree it together, and from the next cone on, the money follows the new split.

## b keeps the paperwork

The partners talk in their own private chat. When they agree something, like Max joining, b drafts it there for everyone to read and approve.

One day the stand may become a proper company. The same record carries over, so they don’t start from scratch.

## What works today

- Automatic splits. Payments split between people the moment they arrive.

- Multisig locks. Funds that take more than one person to move.

- Token rooms. A private chat for the people who hold a token.

Coming: Partnership shares, which tie these together. They aren’t built yet.

Update, 15 Oct 2026: partnership shares are being built and tested on a development branch, not in the current release (5.2.24) and not open to anyone. They need the partner lock finished and tested with real keys, the server changes deployed, and the owner’s sign-off.

Related: [Digital Ice-Cream](https://bwalletx.com/digital-ice-cream) · [Partnership shares](https://bwalletx.com/partnership-shares)

# bShares: a register for any company

bShares keeps a company’s register of members, lets directors approve new shares, and locks shares so they can’t move without the right people. It’s in testing; the first register is our own company.

bShares is a record-keeping tool for any company. It’s in testing; the first register is our own company, The Bitcoin Corporation Ltd.

## The register

Every company keeps a register of members: who holds shares, and how many. bShares keeps it, and shows every change with a date and who approved it.

## Directors approve

New shares are only allotted when the directors approve. bShares records the approval next to the change, so the register and the decision always match.

## Two kinds of lock

- The company’s treasury sits behind a 2-of-3 lock. Two of three keys are needed to move anything.

- Each member’s shares sit behind a 2-of-2 lock held by the company and the member. Neither can move them alone. There’s also a timed way out, so a member is never stuck if the company stops answering.

## From a token to a company

Most things start small: a token, then a room of people around it. Some become partnerships, with [Partnership shares](https://bwalletx.com/partnership-shares). A few become companies. bShares is the last step: the record a company keeps.

Nothing here is an offer of shares.

Related: [bShares](https://bwalletx.com/bshares) · [Partnership shares](https://bwalletx.com/partnership-shares)

# Sign in with HandCash, and invites with tokens

New accounts can now start with HandCash as well as X. Your HandCash handle carries over as name@bwalletx.com, your friends can come with you, and invites with tokens bring people into Spaces.

## Sign in with HandCash

“Sign in with HandCash” now sits next to “Sign in with X” when you make a new account. If you already use HandCash, you don’t need to start from nothing.

- Your handle carries over. Your HandCash handle becomes your paymail: name@bwalletx.com.

- Your friends can come too. Bring your HandCash friends into your bWalletX address book.

Your bWalletX keys are your own, made on your device, as with any other account.

## Your address book, in and out

You can import an address book and export yours. It’s your list, and you can take it with you. This is in bWalletX 5.2.25.

## Invites with tokens

Invites come in two kinds. An Open Drop is a link holding some of a room’s token: the first person to open it claims it. A Named Invite is for one person: only the X account you name can claim it, and the token is sent to them automatically.

Either way, the person signs in with X or HandCash, gets bWalletX, and the token is their ticket into the Space.

## Keep it safe

- An Open Drop link carries the token: whoever opens it first claims it.

- A Named Invite works only for the X account it names.

- We never hold the tokens. They go from the host’s wallet to yours.

## Status, 15 Oct 2026

- ✓ Address book import (CSV, contact cards, JSON, pasted lists) and export to CSV: in the app, shipping in 5.2.25

- ✓ Sign in with HandCash on bchatx.com: switched on; first real sign-in being tested

- ✓ HandCash friends into your address book: the server side is live; the wallet button is coming

- ✓ Open Drops: live in bWalletX 5.2.25 (first run pending). Each link is made for an @handle; whoever opens it first gets the token, and room entry is tied to that X account

- ◻ Named Invites: the token sent automatically to the X account you name. Planned; depends on pre-signed payments

- ◻ Import the people you follow on X: planned

- ◻ Contacts auto-match to paymails as friends join: planned

More on the [Invites](https://bwalletx.com/invite) page.

The first room to use invites is The Scammer Cartel. Its people will come in through invites, straight into the room’s chat and its Space: [bchatx.com/s/scammerscartel](https://chat.bwalletx.com/s/scammerscartel).

[Development blog](https://bwalletx.com/blog) · 058 · 17 Oct 2026

# We could move your name. Now you can see if we do.

A bWalletX name is a row in our database, so we could point it at another key. On 17 Oct we did, for the owner’s own names. Now names are signed by their owners, and every change goes in a public log.

## What happened

Our owner, Richard, has two wallets. Two of his names, `npg@bwalletx.com` and `ninjapunkgirls@bwalletx.com`, were on the wrong one. Early on 17 October he asked us to move them. We did it the quick way: we edited the name directory in our database by hand. A few minutes later we gave a third name, `npgx`, to his NPGX wallet the same way.

Nothing else changed hands. No coins moved. Nobody lost anything. The names were his, on his wallets, at his request.

But it took one line of SQL. And no one outside could have seen it.

## Why that matters

bWalletX never holds your keys or your coins. Payments go from one wallet to another. That part is true and stays true.

Your name is different. `alice@bwalletx.com` is a row in our database that says which key the name points to. If we, or someone who broke into our server, pointed that row at another key, future payments to `$alice` would go there instead. Past payments are safe. Future ones are not.

Every paymail service works this way. We had not said it out loud. Moving the owner’s names made it obvious, so we fixed what we could the same day, and we are saying it now.

## What we built

Signed names. Your wallet now signs a short statement: “this name points to my key, version 1”. Our name server hands that out with your key. We can’t make that signature for a key we don’t hold. Before any payment to a bWalletX name, the paying wallet checks it:

- Signed by its owner: all good.

- Not signed by its owner yet: a grey note; the payment still goes. Wallets sign their own names the next time they open.

- Bad signature: the payment is blocked.

A public name log. Every change of who a name points to is written to a log that can only be added to. Each entry carries the hash of the one before. The database writes the entries itself, so even a hand edit by us is logged, marked `admin`. Anyone can read it:

``curl https://pay.bwallet.space/api/paymail/name-log
curl "https://pay.bwallet.space/api/paymail/name-log?alias=npg"``

The first three entries are our edits from 17 October: two moves and one new name, all marked `admin`, each with a note saying why.

## Standing on others’ work

Signed names are not our idea. [BRC-169](https://github.com/bsv-blockchain/BRCs/blob/master/peer-to-peer/0169.md) already binds handles to keys with a certificate from the host, and warns before paying a name whose key has changed; we plan to adopt that warning too. [BRC-174](https://github.com/bsv-blockchain/BRCs/blob/master/tokens/0174.md) specifies on-chain names held in your wallet, which is where we are headed. The [paymail standard](https://tsc.bsvblockchain.org/standards/paymail/) already lists “alias reassignment” by whoever has the server and database. And public logs that keep operators honest come from [Certificate Transparency](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9162).

Our part is small: the owner signs, not the host; the signature rides in the paymail answer wallets already fetch; and the log catches our own database edits.

## What this doesn’t fix yet

- We still serve the signatures and the log. We could hold a signature back; the name would then show “not signed”.

- We could serve an older genuine signature; its version number would give it away against the log.

- Until the log is anchored on chain, it lives in our database. The hash chain shows tampering only to someone who kept an earlier copy.

## What’s next

Once a day, the log’s latest hash goes into a Bitcoin transaction, so no one can rewrite it after the fact, us included. And for names that must never depend on us, OpNS names live on chain in your own wallet.

We have also written the scheme up as a draft, so any paymail service could sign its names the same way. We have raised it with the authors of BRC-169 and BRC-174 in [BRCs issue #329](https://github.com/bsv-blockchain/BRCs/issues/329), asking whether it belongs inside their work.

## Status, 17 Oct 2026

- ✓ Signed names: wallets sign their own names and check names before paying

- ✓ Bad signatures block payment

- ✓ Public name log, hash-chained, with our 17 Oct edits as its first entries

- ✓ Handovers need both wallets: the owner releases, the new wallet accepts

- ✓ No back door for lost keys

- ✓ Key-change warning before paying

- ✓ Proposed to the BRC authors ([issue #329](https://github.com/bsv-blockchain/BRCs/issues/329))

- ◻ Daily on-chain anchor of the log

- ◻ OpNS names in the wallet

How to check a name yourself, with code: [Signed names](https://bwalletx.com/name-bindings).

Related: [Signed names](https://bwalletx.com/name-bindings) · [Names](https://bwalletx.com/names) · [Handles](https://bwalletx.com/handles) · [Identity](https://bwalletx.com/identity)

Source: https://bwalletx.com/blog/059-b-aware

[Development blog](https://bwalletx.com/blog) · 059 · 20 Oct 2026

# b-Aware: find a hole in bWalletX, get paid in BSV

bWalletX now has a responsible disclosure policy and a bug bounty, paid in BSV. Here is how it works, why the numbers are what they are, and what we did about today’s BRC-100 advisory.

bWalletX is a non-custodial wallet. If it signs something you did not approve, or lets someone read your keys, that is the worst thing it can do, and we would rather hear about it from a researcher than from a victim. So from today there is a page for that: [bwalletx.com/b-Aware](https://bwalletx.com/b-Aware).

## What it is

A responsible disclosure policy and a bug bounty, paid in BSV.

- Report by email to [support@bwalletx.com](mailto:support@bwalletx.com?subject=b-Aware) with the subject `b-Aware`. We acknowledge within 2 working days, give you a severity and a fix plan within 7, and tell you when the fix ships. Never send a recovery phrase or key; use a throwaway wallet to show the problem.

- Rewards: Critical 10 BSV (take funds, extract keys, sign without approval), High 3 BSV (bypass an approval or permission, forge a pairing, drain through a dApp endpoint), Medium 0.5 BSV (leak private data, defeat the safety filter, lock a user out of their own wallet). Low findings get credit.

- Safe harbour. Good-faith research under the policy is authorised. We will not pursue legal action for it, and if someone else does, we will say publicly that you were acting under the policy.

The machine-readable version is at [/.well-known/security.txt](https://bwalletx.com/.well-known/security.txt), and the policy lives in the open-source repository as [SECURITY.md](https://github.com/bitcoin-corp/bwallet/blob/main/SECURITY.md). Ordinary bugs still go to [Bugs](https://bwalletx.com/bugs): tell b in the app.

## Why the numbers look like this

We are a small company and we will not pretend otherwise. A flat “10 BSV per bug” would be the wrong shape now that AI-assisted scanning makes a plausible report nearly free to produce: it would pay a cosmetic finding the same as a key-extraction bug and it would be gamed within a week.

So the programme pays by impact on users’ money and keys, not by count. There is a pool of 20 BSV per calendar quarter; when it is spent, valid reports still earn credit and are paid from the next quarter, in triage order. First valid report of an issue wins. Duplicates, things we already know about and the published “known and accepted” list earn credit, not money. A working reproduction is required.

Ten criticals in a non-custodial wallet would be an existential finding whatever we paid for them. If they exist, we want to know. The pool keeps the spending from running ahead of our ability to fix.

## Public responses to advisories

The page also carries our dated responses to published advisories that touch BRC-100 wallets and the BSV TypeScript stack, because “are we affected?” is the question every wallet user has and few wallets answer in writing.

Today’s entry is [bsv-blockchain/bsv-desktop#135](https://github.com/bsv-blockchain/bsv-desktop/pull/135), a hardening of the reference desktop wallet’s `manifest.json` fetch against server-side request forgery. A BRC-100 wallet fetches an app’s manifest to show its declared permissions in one grouped prompt; in the Electron wallet that fetch ran in the privileged main process on a URL the renderer supplied.

bWalletX is not affected by the same mechanism. There is no page-to-wallet “fetch this URL” channel. The manifest fetch happens inside the wallet toolbox’s permissions manager, which builds the URL from the originator rather than accepting one, goes through the SDK’s public-HTTPS fetch (HTTPS only, no credentials, pinned to that origin), refuses redirects, caps the body and times out. And the originator is not the page’s to choose: the extension rejects any message whose originator does not match the browser-reported sender origin, and the mobile app derives it from the verified origin of each site’s endpoint. The only host a site can make the wallet contact is its own.

We also say what we share with upstream: in browser runtimes the wallet cannot pre-resolve DNS, so a site could rebind its own hostname to a private address. That is listed under “known and accepted” rather than hidden. The two earlier ts-stack advisories (September’s coordinated trust-boundary advisory and July’s createAction output-redirection issue) are patched by the SDK and toolbox versions we ship.

## What we ask of you

Test against your own wallets and your own money. Do not touch anyone else’s data. Give us time to fix before you publish. In return you get a fast, written answer, a reward if it is real, and your name on the page if you want it there.

The credits section is empty today. Yours could be the first name on it.

## Status, 20 Oct 2026

- ✓ Policy, reward table and 20 BSV quarterly pool published at [/b-Aware](https://bwalletx.com/b-Aware)

[Development blog](https://bwalletx.com/blog) · 060 · 24 Oct 2026

# bVideoX: your YouTube videos, on Bitcoin, in your name

You made every one of those videos. bVideoX lets you keep a record of each one in your own wallet: its title, description, date and link, signed and dated on Bitcoin. Three steps: Connect bWalletX, Link YouTube, Mint.

## 1. Connect bWalletX

Go to [bvideox.com](https://bvideox.com) and connect your wallet. Your studio opens at [bvideox.com/studio](https://bvideox.com/studio) under your full paymail, like `name@bwalletx.com`. It also has a public page at `bvideox.com/u/<name>`, and you can pick a different username for that link. Your wallet signs the change, so only you can make it.

## 2. Link YouTube

Link your channel either way: sign in with Google, or paste a short code in your channel description. Only the channel’s verified owner can mint its videos.

For the code, enter your channel and bVideoX gives you a short code. Paste it into your YouTube channel description and press Check. We read your public channel page, find the code, and your wallet signs once to link the channel to you. The code only works for your wallet, and only for 30 minutes. Once the check passes you can delete it from your description.

Then your whole library appears on the page: every public video you’ve posted.

## 3. Mint one, a few, or all of them

Tick the videos you want, or Select all. There is no cap. Each video becomes a record on Bitcoin in your own name, holding its title, description, date, link and a fingerprint of that information.

Records are private by default. They are locked with your wallet’s own keys, so only your 12 words open them. You can make any single record public later, if you want the world to see it.

## What it costs

About 1¢ (1p) per video, plus a tiny network fee. The page shows the total before you mint, and one approval in your wallet covers the batch. A video only shows as done once the network shows the transaction, never just because the wallet said so.

## Your videos stay where they are

bVideoX never downloads or copies your videos. They stay on YouTube and play with YouTube’s own player. What goes on Bitcoin is the record that they’re yours, and when you made them.

Anyone can look around first. [Browse](https://bvideox.com/browse) lists the channels on bVideoX, and you don’t need a wallet to watch. The [privacy](https://bvideox.com/privacy) and [terms](https://bvideox.com/terms) pages say, in plain English, what we read, what we keep and how to remove it.

## Live today, 24 Oct 2026

- ✓ Connect bWalletX: your studio, under your full paymail

- ✓ Link your channel by signing in with Google, or with a short code in its description

- ✓ Your whole library on one page; mint one, some or all

- ✓ Private records locked with your keys; make any one public later

- ✓ Choose your own studio username

- ✓ Browse, Privacy and Terms pages

Related: [bVideoX](https://bvideox.com) · [Get bWalletX](https://bwalletx.com/get) · [Signed names](https://bwalletx.com/blog/058-signed-names)

# Development blog

How bWallet and bWalletX were built, one chapter at a time. Every post is written from the git history of the wallet, this site, the chat server and the PNEEs prototype. It covers what we built, why, what broke, what we reversed and what is still not done.

Newest first. Dates come from commits. bWallet is a fork of [Yours Wallet](https://github.com/yours-org/yours-wallet) (MIT licence).

# Privacy Policy

bWalletX (Beta) · Effective 6 October 2026 · Updated 25 October 2026

bWalletX is published by The Bitcoin Corporation Ltd and is based on the open-source Yours Wallet (MIT licence).
It is not made, reviewed or endorsed by the Yours Wallet authors. This policy covers bWalletX (the full-feature
app, Chrome extension and web wallet) and bWallet, the edition on the App Store and Google Play.

## Summary

bWalletX is non-custodial: your private keys and recovery phrase never leave your device, and we can't move your
money. To run chat, names, contacts and calls, our own service (bChatX, operated by The Bitcoin Corporation
Ltd) keeps the data listed under
[What our service keeps](#service), linked to your wallet's identity key. If you use bChat on a
phone, our push server also keeps your device's push token and notification settings so it can notify you (see
[Notifications](#push)). We use all of this only to run those features. Conversations with b, our
assistant, are different: b is our team, and we read and keep them to fix bugs and improve the app (see
[Conversations with b](#b)). We don't collect your email
address, phone number, location, advertising identifiers, analytics or crash
reports, and we don't track you, sell your data or use it for advertising.

## What stays on your device

-
Your private keys and recovery phrase, encrypted with a key derived from your password and stored in the iOS
Keychain (this device only, excluded from iCloud and device backups) or in Android storage encrypted with an
Android Keystore key (excluded from Google backups).

-
If you turn on Face ID, Touch ID or fingerprint unlock, a key to unlock your wallet is sealed behind your
device's biometrics. Your biometric data itself is handled by the operating system and is never available to
the app.

- Settings, recent sites and apps you open, chat history cached for bChat, and local caches.

## What the app sends over the network

To work as a wallet, the app connects to these third-party services, all over HTTPS:

-
Wallet storage: by default, your wallet's transaction records (outputs, transactions and related
metadata, not your private keys) are synced to a remote wallet storage service operated by 1Sat
(`wallet.1sat.app`). You can change the storage provider in Settings → Wallet Backup.

-
Blockchain services: address, balance, transaction and token lookups, and transaction broadcasts, go to
BSV indexing services (1Sat APIs). Some address-history lookups (when you move funds in from another wallet),
transaction checks and the BSV price history use the WhatsOnChain API, and transaction links open on
WhatsOnChain. The BSV price comes from public price feeds.

- Wallet messaging: wallet-to-wallet messages use `messagebox.1sat.app`.

-
Market, Media, Apps and Chat: trending tokens, collections, listings and ordinal media are loaded from
1Sat indexing and content services (ORDFS). The Apps tab lists bApps such as bChat, bMovies and bWriter; bChat
and other bApps you open talk to their own services, which receive what you send them.

-
Names and payments to names: when you send to a $handle, paymail or OpNS name, or look up your own
name, the app asks 1Sat indexers (including OpNS), bChatX and the paymail service of the address's domain
(for example HandCash for `@handcash.io`) to resolve that name to a payment destination. Those
services see the name being looked up.

-
Market and Chat: token and NFT listings, media and token rooms are loaded from 1Sat indexers. The
Market's safety filter runs as part of that loading; if you use Report, the item is hidden on your device and,
where a review service is configured, the item reference is sent to us for review.

-
Feed: public on-chain posts are loaded from a public bmap indexer and from our own bChat indexer
(`push.bwalletx.com/feed`). Posting puts your post on the public blockchain.

-
$b assistant (optional): nothing is sent until you allow it in the app. In bWallet from the App Store
and Google Play, $b uses your own AI provider key (Anthropic, OpenAI or OpenRouter) and your message and the
recent conversation go straight from your phone to that provider. In bWalletX's pay-per-message mode, they go
to our server (bChatX), which passes them to Anthropic; our server also sees the payment's
transaction id and your bChat sign-in, and Anthropic does not. Your keys, balances, addresses, contacts, chats
and files are never sent. You can withdraw consent in Settings › b agent. What we keep from these
conversations is under [Conversations with b](#b).

-
Websites you open in the in-app browser receive the requests you make and the responses you approve.
They're governed by their own privacy policies.

These services see your IP address and the public blockchain data needed to answer each request. Blockchain
transactions are public by nature.

## What our service keeps

Chat, names, contacts and calls run on bChatX (`bchatx.com`; formerly bit-sign and bitcoinchat.online), operated by The Bitcoin
Corporation Ltd. When you use those features it stores:

- Your identifiers: your wallet's identity key, your $handle and your paymail name.

- Your name: the display name you choose.

- Messages: chat-room and direct messages you send, and room posts.

-
Contacts: the contacts, friends and blocked users you keep in the app (not your phone's address book).

- Other content you create: bookmarks, and items you report for review.

-
Wallet details for rooms and tickets: your wallet addresses and the token holdings needed to check
access to token rooms and tickets.

Calls connect your device directly to the other person's; the service only helps the two devices find each other
and doesn't record calls. All of this is used only to provide these features. It is not shared with third
parties except the hosting providers that run the service, and it is never used for advertising or tracking. You
can delete your account and this data from Settings (Delete account), or by contacting us.

## Conversations with b

b is the bWalletX team's assistant: an AI model (Claude, from Anthropic) run by our server at The Bitcoin
Corporation Ltd, answering on our behalf. When you talk to b, you are talking to our company. Chats with b aren't
secret from us, because b is us. They travel encrypted over HTTPS, and our team reads them so we can help you.
Your keys and 12 words are different: they never leave your device.

-
What we keep: the messages you send b and b's replies, linked to your account, on our server.

-
Why: to fix bugs and improve the app. We are a small team and we read what people tell b so we can act
on it quickly. We never sell conversations, and we don't use them for advertising.

- Improving b: We may use conversations, with personal details removed, to improve b. You can opt out: email [support@bwalletx.com](mailto:support@bwalletx.com?subject=b%20opt-out) with the subject ‘b opt-out’ and we’ll exclude your chats.

- Who can read them: only our team and our server.

- How long: up to 180 days, then they are deleted.

-
Secrets removed: the wallet strips anything that looks like a recovery phrase or private key before a
message leaves your device, and our server strips secrets again before anything is kept. Never type your
recovery phrase, private keys or passwords to b.

-
AI provider: each message, with the recent conversation, is sent to our AI provider (Anthropic) to
write b's reply. If you use your own AI key instead, your messages go from your device to the provider you
chose, under its terms.

-
Deletion: email [support@bwalletx.com](mailto:support@bwalletx.com) to ask us to delete
your conversations with b.

We are rolling out this storage on our server now; we describe it here before it is fully live. More at [bwalletx.com/ask-b](https://bwalletx.com/ask-b#b-is-us).

## Verified identity (KYC certificates)

Identity verification is optional. If you choose to verify, you are sent to bChatX, which uses Veriff to check
your identity document. bChatX and Veriff keep the verification record under their own privacy policies.
bChatX then issues a private certificate that is stored in your wallet on your device. bWalletX does not
upload that certificate anywhere by itself: you choose which details, if any, to reveal to an app or service,
and only when you approve it.

## Link your accounts (bWalletX only)

Creating a wallet needs no social account. Later, you can choose to link X, Google, GitHub, LinkedIn or HandCash
under Settings › Identity › Link your accounts. You sign in on that service in your browser and it confirms the
account is yours. Your wallet then signs the link with its identity key, so a badge on your profile shows it.
The link keeps a one-way hash of the account id and, where there is one, the public handle: your X @name, GitHub
login or HandCash $handle. For LinkedIn the badge shows your display name. For Google we keep only an "email
verified" tick: your email address is never stored, shown or put into a handle. The link is saved on your device
and the bWalletX paymail server (run by The Bitcoin Corporation Ltd) keeps a public copy so others can see the
badge. We don't receive your passwords for these services, and we don't post anything or read anything else from
your accounts. Linked accounts never hold or unlock your keys. You can unlink an account on the same screen. This
option isn't in bWallet from the App Store and Google Play.

## Passkey wallets

If you create or protect a wallet with a passkey, an encrypted copy of your recovery phrase is made so you can
restore with that passkey. It can only be opened with your passkey, which stays in your passwords app or device.
The copy is kept on your device and in the recovery file you save, and our service (bChatX) keeps a copy of the
encrypted data, without any device label or wallet address, so you can restore on a new device. We can't read
it. Removing the passkey in Settings deletes the copy on your device. To ask us to delete the server copy, email
[support@bwalletx.com](mailto:support@bwalletx.com).

## Notifications

On-device alerts. If you allow notifications, the app shows local alerts about incoming transactions.
They're generated on your device.

Push notifications (bChatX). When you're signed in to bChatX, the app registers your device with our push
server, `push.bwalletx.com`, run by The Bitcoin Corporation Ltd on a server we rent from Hetzner, so
you can be told about room mentions and direct messages while the app is closed. On a phone this is on by
default once you sign in to bChat, and your phone asks for permission first; in the web wallet and Chrome
extension it stays off until you turn it on. To do this the app sends:

- the device push token issued by your phone (or, in a browser, the Web Push subscription);

- the platform (iOS, Android, web or extension), the app (bWallet or bWalletX) and its bundle id;

- the bChat handle the device belongs to (your bChat sign-in);

-
your notification preferences: message previews, quiet hours and your time zone, which kinds of alerts you
want, and per-room settings (All, Mentions or Off).

We use this only to send you those notifications. The notification itself is delivered through Google Firebase
Cloud Messaging (Android), Apple Push Notification service (iPhone) or your browser's push service, which
receive the push token and the notification.
Message previews are off by default: a notification then says only that you have something new, without
the message text. If you turn previews on, the message text passes through those services to show it on your
screen.

Turn push off or change previews, quiet hours and alerts in Settings › Notifications › Push notifications, or in
your phone's notification settings. Turning push off, signing out of bChat or switching to another account
removes this device's registration from our push server; uninstalling the app makes its push token stop working.

## Testing waitlist (this website)

If you join the testing waitlist on this website, we collect your email address, the phone platform you chose
(iPhone, Android or Either), the time you signed up, and your browser's user-agent string (to help spot abuse).
This is stored by The Bitcoin Corporation Ltd in our own database and is used only to invite you to test bWallet
and send testing updates. We do not sell it or share it for marketing. You can unsubscribe from any email, or
ask us to delete your entry at any time using the contact details below.

## Paid testers programme and tester check-ins

If you apply at [bwalletx.com/testers](https://bwalletx.com/testers), you sign in with Google and we keep
your Google-verified email address, name and profile photo, the Android phone model you type, the X or GitHub
name you give (optional), the BSV address you want to be paid to, the time you applied and your IP address (to
spot duplicate applications). It is stored by The Bitcoin Corporation Ltd on our server
(`push.bwalletx.com`, Hetzner) and used only to run the programme: approving testers, adding your email
to the Google Play test list, and paying you.

Tester check-ins. Only in the Google Play build, and only after you enter your tester code (or email) in
Settings › Testing, the app sends one check-in a day while it is open: a random install id made on your
phone, your tester code or email, which app store installed it (so we know it came from Google Play) and the app
version. It sends nothing about your keys, addresses, balances or activity. Unlink in Settings › Testing to
stop. Payment never depends on ratings or reviews. Ask us to delete your tester record at any time.

## Your choices

- You can delete your account and the data our service keeps from Settings (Delete account).

- You can delete all app data on your device by signing out in Settings, or by uninstalling the app.

- You can turn biometric unlock off from the lock screen at any time.

-
You can turn push notifications and message previews off in Settings › Notifications, and remove this device's
push registration by signing out of bChat.

- You can withdraw consent for the $b assistant in Settings › b agent, and ask us to delete your conversations with b by emailing support@bwalletx.com.

- You can change the remote wallet storage provider in Settings → Wallet Backup.

## Children

The app is not directed at children under 13.

We'll post changes to this policy on this page, and in the source repository at
[github.com/bitcoin-corp/bwallet](https://github.com/bitcoin-corp/bwallet).

# Add Sign in with bWalletX to your app

Source: https://bwalletx.com/connect (this file: https://bwalletx.com/connect.md). Last checked against bWalletX 5.2.31, connect.js and @bwalletx/connect 0.5.0 on 18 Oct 2026. Full docs: https://docs.bwalletx.com/developers/connect/

## In 30 seconds

One script tag on your page, two routes on your server.

```html
<script src="https://bwalletx.com/connect.js"></script>
```

- `bWalletX.renderButton('#signin', { onClick })` draws the gold "Sign in with bWalletX" button.
- `bWalletX.signIn({ challenge, pairing })` finds the user's wallet (Chrome extension, the bWalletX app's browser, or a phone or the web wallet by QR code), asks your server for a one-time challenge, and has the wallet sign it with a key derived from its **identity key**.
- Your server checks the signature with `@bsv/sdk`, deletes the nonce, and signs the user in as that identity key.
- No API key, no client ID, no account with us. Nothing passes through bwalletx.com except the script itself. The only service of ours involved is the encrypted pairing relay, and only when the user signs in from a phone or the web wallet.

The user's identity key (a 33-byte compressed public key, 66 hex characters) is their user ID on your site. It is the same key every time they sign in with the same wallet.

## Three ways the user's wallet can answer

| Where the user is | How your page reaches the wallet | What you need |
|---|---|---|
| Chrome or Brave with the bWalletX extension | BRC-100 wallet discovery: dispatch `brc100:requestWallet`, take the `brc100:announceWallet` reply whose `info.rdns` is `com.bwalletx.extension` | Nothing extra. connect.js finds it |
| Your site opened inside the bWalletX app's own browser | Same discovery; the app announces `rdns: space.bwallet.mobile` and also sets `window.CWI` | Nothing extra. connect.js finds it |
| bWalletX on a phone, or the web wallet at web.bwalletx.com | Pairing: your page shows a `https://www.bwallet.space/pair?...` link as a QR code. The phone scans it; the web wallet takes it pasted. Both then talk to your page through `relay.bwallet.space`, end-to-end encrypted | A `pairing` option with somewhere to show the QR code. connect.js does the rest |

All three give you the same thing: an object with the BRC-100 `WalletInterface` methods. Sign-in is the same code for all of them.

## 1. Browser: one script tag

`connect.js` is small. It loads the full sign-in build (`https://bwalletx.com/connect/bwalletx-connect.global.js`, about 125 KB with `@bsv/sdk` inside) the first time you call `signIn`, `pair` or `renderButton`, so those three return promises. This example uses qrcodejs from cdnjs to draw the QR code; any QR library works.

```html
<div id="signin"></div>
<div id="bwx-pair"></div>

<script src="https://bwalletx.com/connect.js"></script>
<script src="https://cdnjs.cloudflare.com/ajax/libs/qrcodejs/1.0.0/qrcode.min.js"></script>
<script>
  const panel = document.getElementById('bwx-pair');

  async function post(url, body) {
    const res = await fetch(url, { method: 'POST', headers: { 'content-type': 'application/json' }, body: JSON.stringify(body) });
    if (!res.ok) throw new Error((await res.json().catch(() => ({}))).error || 'HTTP ' + res.status);
    return res.json();
  }

  bWalletX.renderButton('#signin', {
    onClick: async (button) => {
      button.disabled = true;
      try {
        const r = await bWalletX.signIn({
          // 1. Your server makes the challenge for this identity key.
          challenge: (identityKey) => post('/auth/bwalletx/challenge', { identityKey }),
          // 2. Only used when there is no extension or in-app browser: phone or web wallet.
          pairing: {
            onLink: (link) => {
              panel.replaceChildren();
              new QRCode(panel, { text: link, width: 220, height: 220 });
              const p = document.createElement('p');
              p.textContent = 'Scan with bWalletX on your phone, or paste this link into web.bwalletx.com: ' + link;
              panel.append(p);
            },
            onCode: (code) => panel.append('Check bWalletX shows ' + code + ', then tap Connect.'),
          },
        });
        // 3. Your server checks the signature and starts a session.
        const { identityKey } = await post('/auth/bwalletx/verify', {
          identityKey: r.identityKey, nonce: r.nonce, signature: r.signature,
        });
        panel.textContent = 'Signed in as ' + identityKey.slice(0, 12) + '…  (via ' + r.method + ')';
      } catch (e) {
        panel.textContent = e.code === 'NOT_FOUND' ? 'bWalletX was not found.' : e.message;
      } finally {
        button.disabled = false;
      }
    },
  });
</script>
```

`bWalletX.signIn` looks for a wallet in this order:

1. The bWalletX Chrome extension (BRC-100 discovery, `rdns` `com.bwalletx.extension`). `method: 'extension'`.
2. The bWalletX app's in-app browser (`rdns` `space.bwallet.mobile`, or `window.CWI` if nothing announced). `method: 'in-app'`.
3. A pairing saved by an earlier sign-in in this browser (in `localStorage` under `bwalletx.connect.pairing.v1`). `method: 'pairing'`.
4. A new pairing, if you passed `pairing`: `onLink` gets a `https://www.bwallet.space/pair?...` link to show as a QR code (and as text for web.bwalletx.com), and `onCode` gets a 4-digit code both screens show. `method: 'pairing'`.

If none of these works it throws an error with `code: 'NOT_FOUND'`. It returns `{ identityKey, signature, nonce, method, wallet }`. Post the first three to your verify route. `wallet` is a BRC-100 `WalletInterface` you can keep using.

Other things on `window.bWalletX`:

| Call | What it does |
|---|---|
| `bWalletX.connect({ timeout })` | The extension only, authenticated: `{ wallet, info, identityKey }`. Rejects with `code: 'NOT_INSTALLED'`. Doesn't load the full build. |
| `bWalletX.pair({ onLink, onCode })` | A wallet paired by QR or pasted link, without signing in. |
| `bWalletX.renderButton(el, { onClick, subtitle })` | The gold button. `subtitle: false` hides the second line. |
| `bWalletX.load()` | The full build's exports (`signInWithBwalletX`, `pairBwalletX`, `restorePairing`, `clearPairing`, `findBwalletX`, ...). |

Prefer to host it yourself? Copy `connect.js` and `connect/bwalletx-connect.global.js` to the same folder structure on your site; connect.js loads the full build from next to itself. It is also on npm: `pnpm add @bwalletx/connect @bsv/sdk`.

## The button

<!-- preview -->

`bWalletX.renderButton()` draws this for you. If you draw your own, use the gold button. Keep the label "Sign in with bWalletX". The logo is at `https://bwalletx.com/logo.svg` (the gold b, viewBox 74 x 100). Don't recolour it; it sits on a black circle so it reads on the gold.

```html
<button type="button" id="bwx-signin" class="bwx-signin">
  <span class="bwx-mark"><img src="https://bwalletx.com/logo.svg" alt="" width="15" height="20"></span>
  <span class="bwx-label">Sign in with bWalletX<small>also works with bWallet</small></span>
</button>
<div id="bwx-pair"></div>
```

```css
.bwx-signin {
  display: inline-flex; align-items: center; gap: 12px;
  min-height: 48px; padding: 10px 22px 10px 10px;
  border: 0; border-radius: 12px; cursor: pointer;
  background: linear-gradient(180deg, #fcd34d, #f59e0b);
  color: #000; text-align: left;
  font: 700 16px/1.2 system-ui, -apple-system, "Segoe UI", sans-serif;
  box-shadow: 0 8px 24px rgba(245, 158, 11, 0.2);
}
.bwx-signin:hover { background: linear-gradient(180deg, #fde68a, #fbbf24); }
.bwx-signin:focus-visible { outline: 2px solid #ffd24d; outline-offset: 3px; }
.bwx-signin:disabled { opacity: 0.6; cursor: wait; }
.bwx-signin .bwx-mark {
  display: inline-flex; align-items: center; justify-content: center;
  width: 32px; height: 32px; border-radius: 50%; background: #000; flex: none;
}
.bwx-signin small { display: block; font-size: 11px; font-weight: 500; color: rgba(0, 0, 0, 0.6); }
```

Put it first among your wallet options. The second line ("also works with bWallet") is optional: bWallet is the store edition of the same wallet and signs in the same way.

## 2. Server: issue and verify challenges

The server half is not in the script (it must run on your server). Install `@bwalletx/connect` and import from `@bwalletx/connect/server`, or copy this file into your project as `bwalletx-server.ts`. Its only dependency is `@bsv/sdk` (2.2 or later, 2.x or 3.x). It is the same code as `@bwalletx/connect/server`, so the two are interchangeable.

```ts
import { ProtoWallet, PublicKey, type WalletProtocol } from '@bsv/sdk';

/** Security level 2, a protocol name used for nothing else. Keep it constant. */
export const LOGIN_PROTOCOL: WalletProtocol = [2, 'bwallet sign in'];
export const CHALLENGE_LIFETIME_MS = 2 * 60 * 1000;

export interface PendingChallenge {
  identityKey: string;
  origin: string;
  message: string;
  expiresAt: number;
}

/**
 * Where challenges wait between the two routes. Use Redis or a database table in production.
 * `take` must read and delete in one step, so each nonce can be tried once.
 */
export interface NonceStore {
  put(nonce: string, c: PendingChallenge): Promise<void> | void;
  take(nonce: string): Promise<PendingChallenge | null> | PendingChallenge | null;
}

let warned = false;

/**
 * In-memory store. For development and tests only: it is lost on restart and not shared between
 * server processes or serverless instances. Expired entries are pruned on each put.
 */
export function memoryStore(opts: { quiet?: boolean } = {}): NonceStore {
  if (!opts.quiet && !warned) {
    warned = true;
    console.warn('[@bwalletx/connect] Using the in-memory nonce store. It is for development only; pass a shared store (Redis, database) in production.');
  }
  const m = new Map<string, PendingChallenge>();
  return {
    put(nonce, c) {
      const now = Date.now();
      for (const [k, v] of m) if (v.expiresAt < now) m.delete(k);
      m.set(nonce, c);
    },
    take(nonce) {
      const c = m.get(nonce) ?? null;
      m.delete(nonce);
      return c;
    },
  };
}

let defaultStore: NonceStore | null = null;
const storeOrDefault = (s?: NonceStore) => s ?? (defaultStore ??= memoryStore());

export function isIdentityKey(x: unknown): x is string {
  if (typeof x !== 'string' || !/^0[23][0-9a-fA-F]{64}$/.test(x)) return false;
  try {
    PublicKey.fromString(x);
    return true;
  } catch {
    return false;
  }
}

function normalOrigin(origin: string): string {
  const u = new URL(origin);
  if (u.origin === 'null' || u.origin !== origin.replace(/\/$/, '')) {
    throw new Error(`origin must be scheme://host[:port], got ${origin}`);
  }
  return u.origin;
}

/** The text the user signs. Lines joined with \n, no trailing newline. */
export function loginMessage(origin: string, nonce: string, expiresAt: number): string {
  return [
    `Sign in to ${new URL(origin).host} with bWallet`,
    '',
    'This proves you hold this wallet. It does not spend anything.',
    '',
    `Origin: ${origin}`,
    `Nonce: ${nonce}`,
    `Expires: ${new Date(expiresAt).toISOString()}`,
  ].join('\n');
}

function randomNonce(): string {
  const b = new Uint8Array(16);
  globalThis.crypto.getRandomValues(b);
  let s = '';
  for (const x of b) s += String.fromCharCode(x);
  return btoa(s).replace(/\+/g, '-').replace(/\//g, '_').replace(/=+$/, '');
}

export interface CreateChallengeOptions {
  /** YOUR site's origin from config, e.g. "https://example.com". Never take it from the request. */
  origin: string;
  /** The identity key the browser claims. Checked again at verify. */
  identityKey: unknown;
  /** Default: a process-wide in-memory store (dev only). */
  store?: NonceStore;
}

export interface ChallengeResponse {
  nonce: string;
  message: string;
  protocolID: WalletProtocol;
  keyID: string;
  expiresAt: number;
}

/** Step 1. Throws if identityKey is not a valid compressed public key. Send the result to the browser. */
export async function createChallenge(opts: CreateChallengeOptions): Promise<ChallengeResponse> {
  if (!isIdentityKey(opts.identityKey)) throw new Error('identityKey must be a compressed public key (66 hex chars)');
  const origin = normalOrigin(opts.origin);
  const nonce = randomNonce();
  const expiresAt = Date.now() + CHALLENGE_LIFETIME_MS;
  const message = loginMessage(origin, nonce, expiresAt);
  await storeOrDefault(opts.store).put(nonce, { identityKey: opts.identityKey.toLowerCase(), origin, message, expiresAt });
  return { nonce, message, protocolID: LOGIN_PROTOCOL, keyID: nonce, expiresAt };
}

export interface VerifySignInOptions {
  /** YOUR site's origin from config. Must equal the origin the challenge was made for. */
  origin: string;
  /** From the request body. */
  identityKey: unknown;
  nonce: unknown;
  signature: unknown;
  store?: NonceStore;
}

/**
 * Step 2. Returns the proven identity key (lowercase hex), or null.
 * The nonce is deleted before anything is checked, so each challenge can be tried once.
 */
export async function verifySignIn(opts: VerifySignInOptions): Promise<string | null> {
  if (typeof opts.nonce !== 'string' || opts.nonce.length > 64) return null;
  const c = await storeOrDefault(opts.store).take(opts.nonce);
  if (!c || Date.now() > c.expiresAt) return null;
  let origin: string;
  try {
    origin = normalOrigin(opts.origin);
  } catch {
    return null;
  }
  if (c.origin !== origin) return null;
  if (!isIdentityKey(opts.identityKey)) return null;
  const identityKey = opts.identityKey.toLowerCase();
  if (c.identityKey !== identityKey) return null;

  const sig = opts.signature;
  if (!Array.isArray(sig) || sig.length < 8 || sig.length > 80 || !sig.every((b) => Number.isInteger(b) && b >= 0 && b <= 255)) {
    return null;
  }
  try {
    const { valid } = await new ProtoWallet('anyone').verifySignature({
      protocolID: LOGIN_PROTOCOL,
      keyID: opts.nonce,
      counterparty: identityKey,
      data: Array.from(new TextEncoder().encode(c.message)),
      signature: sig as number[],
    });
    return valid ? identityKey : null;
  } catch {
    return null; // @bsv/sdk throws on a bad signature instead of returning valid: false
  }
}

/** True when a request's Origin header is exactly your configured origin. Check it on both routes. */
export function originAllowed(requestOrigin: string | null | undefined, origin: string): boolean {
  try {
    return !!requestOrigin && requestOrigin === normalOrigin(origin);
  } catch {
    return false;
  }
}
```

Two routes. This example uses Express; any framework works the same way.

```ts
// Two routes (Express). Any framework works the same way.
import express from 'express';
import { createChallenge, verifySignIn, originAllowed, memoryStore } from './bwalletx-server.js';

const ORIGIN = 'https://example.com'; // your site, from config. Never from the request.
const store = memoryStore();          // dev only: use Redis or a database table in production
const app = express();
app.use(express.json());

// POST /auth/bwalletx/challenge   body: { identityKey }
app.post('/auth/bwalletx/challenge', async (req, res) => {
  if (!originAllowed(req.get('origin'), ORIGIN)) return res.status(403).end();
  try {
    res.json(await createChallenge({ origin: ORIGIN, identityKey: req.body?.identityKey, store }));
  } catch (e) {
    res.status(400).json({ error: (e as Error).message });
  }
});

// POST /auth/bwalletx/verify   body: { identityKey, nonce, signature }
app.post('/auth/bwalletx/verify', async (req, res) => {
  if (!originAllowed(req.get('origin'), ORIGIN)) return res.status(403).end();
  const identityKey = await verifySignIn({ origin: ORIGIN, store, ...req.body });
  if (!identityKey) return res.status(401).json({ error: 'That signature was not accepted. Start again.' });
  // identityKey is the user's stable id. Find or create the account keyed on it, then start your session.
  res.json({ identityKey });
});

app.listen(3000);
```

`verifySignIn` returns the identity key (66 lowercase hex characters) or `null`. It refuses a nonce that was already used, has expired (2 minutes), was issued for another origin or another identity key, or whose signature doesn't verify.

`memoryStore()` is for development: it is lost on restart and isn't shared between processes or serverless instances. In production pass a store whose `take(nonce)` reads and deletes in one step, such as Redis `GETDEL` or a database `DELETE ... RETURNING`.

## Exactly what is signed

The server builds this text, sends it to the browser, and keeps a copy. The wallet signs the UTF-8 bytes of it unchanged. Lines are joined with `\n`, no trailing newline.

```
Sign in to example.com with bWallet

This proves you hold this wallet. It does not spend anything.

Origin: https://example.com
Nonce: 3q2-7wEXAMPLEnonce0Q8w
Expires: 2026-10-07T12:02:00.000Z
```

(The second and fourth lines are empty.) This is the same text bChat and bit-sign use. The wallet does not parse it; any text works, but keep your origin, the nonce and the expiry in it so the user can see what they are approving and a signature made for your site is worthless anywhere else.

The signature call, as the wallet receives it:

| Field | Value |
|---|---|
| `protocolID` | `[2, 'bwallet sign in']` (security level 2: the derived key depends on the counterparty) |
| `keyID` | the nonce |
| `counterparty` | `'anyone'` |
| `data` | the UTF-8 bytes of the text, as `number[]` |
| result `signature` | DER-encoded ECDSA signature, as `number[]` |

The signing key is derived (BRC-42) from the wallet's root identity private key towards "anyone", for that protocol and keyID. Anyone holding only the identity public key can derive the matching public key, which is what `new ProtoWallet('anyone').verifySignature({ ..., counterparty: identityKey })` does (BRC-3). Only the holder of the identity private key can make the signature.

## Security notes

- **One try per nonce.** Delete the challenge before you check the signature, as `verifySignIn` does. A challenge that survives a failed attempt can be retried.
- **Two-minute expiry.** Check it on the server. Don't trust an expiry sent by the browser.
- **The nonce is also the keyID,** so each challenge is signed by a different derived key. A signature for one nonce can't be used for another.
- **Build the text on the server** and verify against your stored copy. Never verify text the browser sends you.
- **Use your configured origin** in the text, not a value from the request. Refuse challenge and verify calls whose `Origin` header isn't your site.
- **Bind the challenge to the identity key** the browser claimed, and check it again at verify.
- **`verifySignature` throws** on a bad signature in @bsv/sdk instead of returning `valid: false`. Catch it and treat it as a failure.
- **Check the key is a real point:** `PublicKey.fromString` throws for a 66-hex string that isn't on the curve.
- **Rate-limit** the challenge route per IP and per identity key. It is unauthenticated.
- **Sessions are yours.** After `verifySignIn` returns a key, issue your normal session cookie. The wallet does not give you a token.
- **Privacy.** The identity key is the same on every site the user signs in to with this method, so two sites can tell it is the same wallet. Tell your users this if it matters to them.
- **Pairing.** The relay checks the WebSocket `Origin` of the page that opened the channel and tells the wallet; the wallet refuses to pair if it differs from the origin in the QR code. The relay only sees ciphertext. The pairing key connect.js makes is random and is not a wallet key.
- **What the user sees.** The extension and the phone show their own approval prompt naming your site's host (taken from the page or the relay, not from your text). Nothing is spent.

## Not yet available

These are gaps today. Plan around them.

- **No hosted sign-in or OAuth-style redirect.** There is no bwalletx.com page you can send users to and get a callback from, and no hosted verify endpoint. You run the two routes yourself. bChat's own endpoints (`/api/bitsign/auth/bwallet/*` on bit-sign) accept requests from their own pages only and are not a public API.
- **No user profile.** You get the identity key and nothing else: no $handle, paymail, name or picture, and no proof linking the key to them.
- **The relay is ours.** `relay.bwallet.space` accepts any https origin, but it is a single service run by The Bitcoin Corporation with no published uptime or rate-limit guarantees (it currently allows about 60 frames a minute per channel).
- **No test wallet.** There is no testnet build or headless bWalletX for automated tests. To test your server, sign with `new ProtoWallet(PrivateKey.fromRandom()).createSignature(...)` using the same arguments; it makes exactly the signature bWalletX makes.

## For AI agents

Follow these steps in order. Do not invent packages, endpoints or methods that are not on this page. For a bundled app, install `@bwalletx/connect` and `@bsv/sdk`; for a plain HTML site, use the script tag.

1. Install `@bwalletx/connect` and `@bsv/sdk` in the server project (pnpm, npm or yarn, whichever the project uses).
2. Create `bwalletx-server.ts` with the code in section 2, unchanged. Put your site's origin (scheme + host, no trailing slash, e.g. `https://example.com`) in config.
3. Add two POST routes. `/auth/bwalletx/challenge`: `createChallenge({ origin: ORIGIN, identityKey: body.identityKey, store })`, return the result as JSON, 400 if it throws. `/auth/bwalletx/verify`: `verifySignIn({ origin: ORIGIN, store, identityKey, nonce, signature })` from the body. Reject both with 403 unless `originAllowed(request Origin header, ORIGIN)`.
4. Replace `memoryStore()` with a shared store (database table or Redis) if you run more than one server process or run serverless. `take(nonce)` must read and delete in one step.
5. In the verify route, when `verifySignIn` returns a key: find the user whose bWalletX identity key equals it, or create one, then start your normal session. Return 401 when it returns null.
6. On the sign-in page add `<script src="https://bwalletx.com/connect.js"></script>` and the code from section 1: `bWalletX.renderButton(...)` with an `onClick` that calls `bWalletX.signIn({ challenge, pairing })` and posts `identityKey`, `nonce` and `signature` to the verify route. Keep the `pairing` option so phone and web wallet users can sign in; draw the QR code with any QR library.
7. If your page uses a bundler, the same calls work: `window.bWalletX` is set once the script tag has loaded.
8. Test the server without a wallet: `const k = PrivateKey.fromRandom()`, call the challenge route with `k.toPublicKey().toString()`, sign the returned `message` with `new ProtoWallet(k).createSignature({ protocolID, keyID, counterparty: 'anyone', data: Array.from(Buffer.from(message, 'utf8')) })`, post `{ identityKey, nonce, signature }` to verify and expect success. Post the same body again and expect 401.
9. Test by hand: with the bWalletX extension in Chrome, click the button and approve. Without it, scan the QR with bWalletX on a phone, check the 4-digit codes match, tap Connect, approve.

Questions: support@bwalletx.com
